hints: pass means "do nothing here". Replace it with a call to print().
Text goes in double quotes: print("…"). The line must be indented by one tab, the same as pass was.

title: Which node does that?
task:
Finish node_for(job) so it returns the name of the node that does each job, as a String:

  • "draw a picture" → "Sprite2D"
  • "count down" → "Timer"
  • "choose what the screen shows" → "Camera2D"
  • "show text" → "Label"
  • "play a sound" → "AudioStreamPlayer"
  • anything else → "Node"

The match statement is already started for you: it compares job with each pattern in turn and runs the first that fits. _ means "anything".
starter:
extends Node

func node_for(job: String) -> String:
	match job:
		"draw a picture":
			return "Sprite2D"
		_:
			return "Node"
solution:
extends Node

func node_for(job: String) -> String:
	match job:
		"draw a picture":
			return "Sprite2D"
		"count down":
			return "Timer"
		"choose what the screen shows":
			return "Camera2D"
		"show text":
			return "Label"

hints: Each new case is two lines: the pattern, ending in a colon, and an indented return under it – copy the shape of the "draw a picture" one.
Keep _: last. match stops at the first pattern that fits, and _ fits everything.

Leave _draw() alone.

func _ready() -> void:

func _draw() -> void:

title: Name the handler
task:
When you connect a signal in the Node dock, the editor proposes a name for the function that will receive it: _on_, then the sending node's name in lower case with underscores, then _, then the signal's name. Connecting pressed from a node called Spin proposes _on_spin_pressed; from MapButton, _on_map_button_pressed.

Write handler_name(node_name, signal_name) so that it returns that name.
hints: Strings join with +. There are four pieces: "_on_", the node's name, "_" and the signal's name.
A String can rewrite itself in that style: "MapButton".to_snake_case() is "map_button".
explain: Node names are written LikeThis and functions like_this; that is Godot's convention, and the editor follows it when it names things for you. The name is only a proposal – you can type any other in the dialog – but keeping it means anybody reading _on_map_button_pressed knows at once which node and which signal call it.

func _ready() -> void:
	scale = Vector2(2, 2)

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_line(Vector2(-16, 0), Vector2(16, 0), Color("#f2c14e"), 3)

	draw_line(Vector2(16, 0), Vector2(8, 7), Color("#f2c14e"), 3)

tests.label: 40 pixels below the middle: (160, 130)
a quarter turn clockwise: 90 degrees
still twice the size

hints: Which way does y grow on a screen? The node starts at (160, 90).
rotation is in radians. Either use the property that counts in degrees, or convert: deg_to_rad(90).
explain: Both bugs come from carrying a habit over from somewhere else: graphs at school, where up is positive, and everyday angles, which are in degrees. Neither one causes an error, which is what makes them slow to find – the game runs, and something is in the wrong place. When a node is not where you expect, print its position and rotation_degrees before you suspect anything cleverer.

title: Snap to the grid
task: With grid snapping on, the viewport moves whatever you drag to the nearest point of a grid. Write snap_to_grid(p, step): it returns p with x and y each moved to the nearest multiple of step. With a step of 16, (203, 77) becomes (208, 80) and (7, 7) becomes (0, 0).

tests.label: a point already on the grid stays where it is
a finer grid: step 8
it works left of the origin too

hints: A Vector2 can snap itself: p.snapped(grid), where grid is a Vector2 holding the step for x and the step for y.
return p.snapped(Vector2(step, step))
explain: You could also do it by hand – divide by the step, round, multiply back – once for x and once for y. snapped is that, built in. Snapping is why level pieces placed in the editor line up exactly, and Little Hours uses the same idea in play: furniture you drop lands on a 6-pixel grid.

title: Run, then Stop
task:
Model the most important thing the simulator showed you: playing never changes the saved scene. scene is what the editor holds. live is the running game's own copy, and is empty when nothing is running.

  • run() fills live with a copy of scene that shares nothing with it.
  • stop() empties live.
  • is_running() is true between the two.

The code below the line plays a short session and is not to be changed. As it stands, playing moves the editor's player – which is the bug.

tests.label: after playing, the saved player has not moved
and the saved coin is still visible
stopping did not empty the saved scene
after stop(), is_running() is false
and live is empty
after run(), is_running() is true
a new run starts from the saved scene again

hints: live = scene does not copy anything: it makes live a second name for the same dictionary. You need a real copy.
scene.duplicate() copies the outer dictionary only – the inner ones for Player and Coin would still be shared. scene.duplicate(true) copies all the way down.
stop() can give live a fresh empty dictionary, live = {}, and is_running() can ask whether it is empty: not live.is_empty().
explain: Godot gets this separation the simplest way there is: the running game is a different program, which loads the scene from the file. Here you had to make the copy yourself, and it showed up a rule that matters all through GDScript: assigning a dictionary or an array gives you another name for the same thing, not a copy. Chapter G spends a whole section on it. In stop(), live = {} is the safe way to empty it; live.clear() works too – but only once run() makes a real copy, or it would wipe the scene as well.

title: What the scene file keeps
task:
Write the part of the editor that saves one node. scene_lines(node_name, type, props, defaults) returns a list of text lines:

  • first, the heading: [node name="Coin" type="Sprite2D" parent="."] with the node's own name and type in it;
  • then one line for each property in props whose value differs from the one in defaults, in the order they appear in props, written name = value;
  • a value that is text is written inside double quotes: text = "Coins: 0".

A node with nothing changed is a heading and no more. _ready() prints two nodes so you can see your lines.

tests.label: Coin: the heading, then z_index and flip_h – visible is still the default
Score: text in double quotes, then visible
nothing changed: the heading alone
the order follows props, not defaults

hints: A double quote inside a double-quoted string is written \". The heading is one format string: "[node name=\"%s\" type=\"%s\" parent=\".\"]" % [node_name, type].
Loop with for key in props:, and skip the ones that match: if props[key] == defaults[key]: continue.
Two ways to write a line. Text: "%s = \"%s\"" % [key, value]. Anything else: "%s = %s" % [key, value]. Choose with if value is String:.
explain: This is very nearly what Godot does when you press Ctrl+S, and it is why you can open a .tscn in any text editor and understand it. It is also why scenes behave well in version control: change one property and one line of the file changes. Run it and compare your output with the simulator's Scene file (.tscn) tab.

title: Write the path
task:
The script builds this tree:

Main
  Room
    Bed
    Lamp
  Player
    Sprite
  HUD
    DayLabel

Fill in the four path strings so that each leads to the right node:

  • main_to_lamp – from Main to Lamp
  • lamp_to_bed – from Lamp to Bed, its sibling
  • player_to_day_label – from Player to DayLabel
  • sprite_to_bed – from Sprite to Bed

Change only the four strings. Run prints what each one finds.

tests.label: main_to_lamp leads from Main to Lamp
lamp_to_bed leads from Lamp to Bed
player_to_day_label leads from Player to DayLabel
sprite_to_bed leads from Sprite to Bed

hints: A path does not include the node you start from. From Main, the first step is one of Main's children.
To reach a sibling, go up to the shared parent and down again: "../Bed". Each further level you have to climb is another ../ on the front.
explain: Count the climbs: Lamp and Bed share a parent, so one ... Player has to reach Main to get to the HUD, also one. Sprite is two below Main, so two. The longer the row of ../, the more your script knows about a tree it does not own – in a real project the last two are jobs for a signal or a group.

title: Is it above me?
task:
Real nodes have is_ancestor_of(node): it answers whether this node is somewhere above the other one – its parent, its grandparent, and so on up. Write it for MiniNode.

main.is_ancestor_of(sprite) and player.is_ancestor_of(sprite) are true. sprite.is_ancestor_of(player) is false – wrong way round – and so is room.is_ancestor_of(sprite), a different branch. A node is not its own ancestor.

tests.label: a parent is an ancestor
so is a grandparent
a child is not an ancestor of its parent
a node in another branch is not an ancestor
a node is not its own ancestor
asking about the top of the tree gives false, not an error

hints: Do not search downwards through children. Start from other and walk up: there is only one way to go.
var above := other.parent, then while above != null: – if above == self return true, otherwise above = above.parent. After the loop, false.
explain: Searching down from self would work too, but it visits every node in the branch. Walking up from other visits at most one node per level. Whenever a tree question can be asked from the bottom, ask it from the bottom. Starting at other.parent, not other, is what makes a node not its own ancestor.

title: Fix the bug: who is ready first?
task:
ready_order(node) should return the names of a branch in the order Godot calls _ready() on them. Before you run it, write down what you expect for the tree below. Then run it: the function is wrong – it gives the order nodes enter the tree, not the order they become ready. Fix it.

Main
  Room
    Bed
    Lamp
  Player
    Sprite
  HUD

tests.label: the whole tree: children before their parents, Main last
the Player branch: Sprite, then Player
a node with no children is ready on its own

hints: Nothing is wrong with the loop. What is wrong is when the node adds its own name.
Start with an empty list, let every child add its names, and append node.name after the loop.
explain: One line moved, and the meaning changed from "me, then my children" to "my children, then me". Notice that Room is ready before Player has even started: Room's whole branch finishes first. That is why a node can use its children in _ready() but cannot count on a sibling lower in the dock.

title: Move house
task:
Write two methods for MiniNode.

  • remove_child(child) takes child out of this node's children and leaves it with no parent. If child is not one of this node's children, nothing changes.
  • reparent(new_parent) moves this node from wherever it is to the end of new_parent's children. It must work for a node that has no parent yet, too.

_ready() already makes three moves and is not to be changed: the lamp is carried from the room to the player, the day label is removed from the HUD, and a new hat is given to the player.

tests.label: the lamp's parent is now Player
Room is left with only the Bed
DayLabel is out of the HUD and has no parent
Room removing Sprite changes nothing: Sprite was never Room's child
Player's children are Sprite, Lamp, Hat, in that order
the Hat, which had no parent, now has one

hints: remove_child undoes both halves of add_child: children.erase(child) and child.parent = null. Guard it first – only if child.parent == self.
reparent is the two methods you already have: if there is a parent, ask it to remove_child(self); then new_parent.add_child(self).
explain: The guard in remove_child is the important line. Without it, room.remove_child(sprite) would set the sprite's parent to null while Player still listed it as a child – the two halves of the link disagreeing, which is the one state a tree must never be in. Godot's real reparent() does one more kind thing: by default it adjusts the node's position so that it does not jump on the screen when its parent changes.

title: Groups from a dictionary
task:
Finish MiniTree, which keeps the groups: a dictionary from a label to the list of nodes carrying it.

  • add_to_group(node, label) – adds the node under that label. Adding the same node twice must not list it twice.
  • get_nodes_in_group(label) – the list for that label, in the order the nodes were added; an empty Array for a label nobody carries.
  • is_in_group(node, label) – true or false.
  • call_group(label, method) – calls the method with that name on every node in the group.

_ready() fills the groups and then hides everything in "lights"; do not change it.

tests.label: lights holds Lamp then Candle – Candle once, though it was added twice
a node can be in more than one group
an unknown label gives an empty Array
is_in_group says yes for members
is_in_group says no for everyone else, and for unknown labels
call_group("lights", "hide") hid both lights
the kettle, not a light, is untouched

hints: In add_to_group, make the list the first time a label is seen: if not groups.has(label): groups[label] = []. Then append only if not groups[label].has(node).
groups.get(label, []) returns the list, or an empty one when the label is missing. is_in_group can be built on that with .has(node).
For call_group: loop over the group, and for each node Callable(node, method).call().
explain: Every method leans on get_nodes_in_group, and because that one answers an unknown label with an empty list, the others need no special case: looping over nothing does nothing, and nothing has no members. Designing the "not there" answer to be harmless, as Godot does here, removes a whole class of checks from the code that calls it.

title: queue_free, and the end of the frame
task:
queue_free() does not delete a node: it marks it, and the tree does the deleting when the frame ends. Model both halves. Marking is done for you – queue_free() sets queued. Write end_of_frame(), which removes every queued node from the tree with its whole branch and returns how many nodes went in total.

In the tree below, _ready() queues Lamp, Player and Sprite. Until end_of_frame() is called all eight nodes must still be there. The first call returns 3 – Lamp, Player and Player's Sprite, counted once – and leaves five. A second call finds nothing to do and returns 0.

Main
  Room
    Bed
    Lamp
  Player
    Sprite
  HUD
    DayLabel

tests.label: before the frame ends, all eight nodes are still in the tree
end_of_frame() removes Lamp, Player and Sprite: 3
five nodes are left
Main's children are Room and HUD
Room keeps the Bed and loses the Lamp
the removed nodes have no parent
a second end_of_frame() has nothing to remove

hints: Write a helper that handles one node's children and calls itself on the ones that stay – sweep(node) -> int – and have end_of_frame() return sweep(main).
For each child: if it is queued, erase it from node.children, clear its parent, and add child.count() to the total. If it is not, add sweep(child).
Removing from a list while looping over that same list skips items. Loop over a copy: for child in node.children.duplicate():.
explain: Two traps are in here. The first is the loop: erase from the list you are walking and the next item slides into the gap and is missed, so you walk a copy. The second is the Sprite, queued inside a queued Player – once Player's branch is removed there is no need to look inside it, and counting the branch with count() counts the Sprite exactly once. The split between marking and sweeping is the point of the real queue_free(): code that runs later in the same frame can still safely touch the node.

title: Right value, wrong type

tests.label: coins is the int 25
speed is the float 2.0
player_name is the String "Wren"
has_key is the bool true

title: Predict, then check
task:
Do not run anything yet. Work out in your head what each of these four expressions gives, and put your answers in the four guess variables – with the right type, so 3 and 3.0 are different guesses. Then press Check.

  • guess_a: 9 / 2
  • guess_b: 9 / 2.0
  • guess_c: 1 / 4 * 4
  • guess_d: 10 / 4 * 2.0
starter:
extends Node

var guess_a = -1
var guess_b = -1
var guess_c = -1
var guess_d = -1
solution:
extends Node

var guess_a = 4
var guess_b = 4.5
var guess_c = 0
var guess_d = 4.0

tests.label: guess_a is what 9 / 2 gives
guess_b is what 9 / 2.0 gives
guess_c is what 1 / 4 * 4 gives
guess_d is what 10 / 4 * 2.0 gives

hints: Work from left to right, one operator at a time, and ask at each one: are both sides ints?
In the last one, 10 / 4 happens first, and both of those are ints. The float arrives too late to save the fraction.

title: Fix the bug: the empty bar
task: The health bar is drawn from health_fraction(), which should give a float from 0.0 (empty) to 1.0 (full). It shows an empty bar until health is completely full. Find the bug and fix it, so that 30 out of 120 gives 0.25.

tests.label: health_fraction(119, 120) is nearly full, not empty

hints: Both health and max_health are ints. What does an int divided by an int give?
Turn one side into a float before the division: float(health) / max_health.
explain: The return type -> float did not save it: the division had already thrown the fraction away, and turning 0 into 0.0 afterwards is no help. The conversion has to happen before the divide. Note that you cannot fix this one by typing 120.0 – the numbers arrive as ints – which is when float() earns its keep.

title: Tiles and pixels
task:
A room is a row of tiles, each TILE pixels wide, numbered from 0 at the left. Finish three functions:

  • tile_of(x) – which tile a pixel position is in, as an int. Pixels 0 up to (but not including) 96 are tile 0, 96 up to 192 are tile 1, and so on.
  • tile_left(col) – the pixel where a tile starts, as an int. Tile 2 starts at 192.
  • tile_centre(col) – the pixel in the middle of a tile, as a float. Tile 0's centre is 48.0.

Use TILE, not 96, so the functions still work when the tile size changes.

tests.label: the functions use TILE, not a typed 96 or 48
tests.why: Only the const line should mention the number. Use TILE everywhere else, and TILE / 2.0 for half a tile.

hints: x / TILE is a float divided by an int, so it keeps its fraction: 95.5 / 96 is 0.99…. Which converter cuts that down to a whole tile number?
For the centre, add half a tile to the left edge. Half of TILE as a float is TILE / 2.0.
explain: Three small conversions between a world measured in pixels and a world counted in tiles: int() to go from a measurement to a count, a multiplication to go back, and a deliberate 2.0 so the centre of an odd-sized tile would still be right. Little Hours does this constantly, with the same TILE.

title: Halfway, and a shade of grey
task:
Two functions on values with parts:

  • midpoint(a, b) – the Vector2 exactly halfway between two points. Halfway between (0, 0) and (10, 20) is (5, 10).
  • grey(level) – a Color whose red, green and blue are all level, so grey(0.0) is black, grey(1.0) is white and grey(0.5) is mid grey.

tests.label: grey() is solid: alpha is 1.0

hints: Vectors add part by part, and dividing a vector by a number divides both parts. Mind the brackets: the adding has to happen first.
(a + b) / 2 and Color(level, level, level).
explain: No .x or .y in sight: the arithmetic works on the whole vector. And / 2 is safe here, because a Vector2's parts are floats – with Vector2i the second check would have given (3, 4).

title: Seasons from a day number
task:
A season lasts DAYS_PER_SEASON days. Days 1 to 5 are spring, 6 to 10 summer, 11 to 15 autumn and 16 to 20 winter. (Only the first year matters here: days 1 to 20.)

  • Add an enum Season with SPRING, SUMMER, AUTUMN and WINTER, in that order.
  • Finish season_of(day) so it returns the right Season value.
  • Finish season_label(day) so it returns the season's name as it is written in the enum: season_label(12) is "AUTUMN".

No if is needed. Think about what integer division does to the day number – and about day 5 and day 6.

tests.label: Season.SPRING is first
Season.WINTER is last
day 5 is still spring
day 6 is the first of summer

hints: day / DAYS_PER_SEASON is nearly right: it gives 0 for days 1 to 4, but 1 for day 5. Days are counted from 1 and division counts from 0. What could you do to the day first?
(day - 1) / DAYS_PER_SEASON gives 0, 1, 2 or 3 – the same numbers the enum gave its names. For the label, Season.keys() is the list of names and [n] picks one.
explain: Integer division doing useful work: it sorts twenty days into four boxes of five. The - 1 is the part people get wrong, and Little Hours's own season_index() and year() both have it for the same reason. Because the enum's values are 0 to 3 in order, the answer to the division is the season. Chapter E adds the piece that makes it work past day 20.

title: Fix the bug: nobody is rich
task: wealth(coins) should answer "rich" from 100 coins up, "comfortable" from 20 to 99, "getting by" from 1 to 19 and "broke" at 0. Every condition in it is correct, and yet somebody with 150 coins is told they are comfortable. Fix it without changing any of the numbers.

A ladder stops at the first true rung, so the narrowest question has to be asked first. Swap the first two rungs, each with its return.
