title: Opening hours
task: The grocer is open from 8 until 18 on days 1 to 5 (Monday to Friday), from 8 until 12 on day 6, and closed all of day 7. "Until 18" means 17 is open and 18 is shut. Finish is_open(hour, day) so that it returns true or false. hour is a whole number from 0 to 23.

tests.label: is_open(7, 1)  →  false: too early
is_open(8, 3)  →  true: 8 itself is open
is_open(18, 5)  →  false: 18 itself is shut
is_open(12, 6)  →  false: Saturday ends at 12
is_open(10, 7)  →  false: closed on day 7

hints: "From 8 until 18" is two comparisons joined with and: hour >= 8 and hour < 18. A comparison is already a bool, so you can return it directly.
Deal with the odd days first: if it is day 7, return false; if it is day 6, return the answer for the short hours; whatever is left is an ordinary day.
explain: There is no if … return true else return false anywhere: the comparison is the answer. And handling the special cases first, each with its own return, leaves the last line free to state the ordinary rule plainly. It can be done in one long expression with brackets; this way is easier to get right.

title: Count the vowels
task: Finish count_vowels(text), which returns how many of the letters in text are vowels: a, e, i, o or u. Capitals count as well, so count_vowels("AEIOU") is 5. Use a for loop over the String.

tests.label: count_vowels("")  →  0: an empty String has none
count_vowels("AEIOU")  →  5: capitals count
uses a for loop

hints: The build-up-an-answer shape: a counter made before the loop, += 1 inside an if, and return after the loop.
letter in "aeiou" asks whether one character is a vowel. For the capitals, loop over text.to_lower() instead of text.
explain: in saved five comparisons joined with or, and to_lower() saved five more. Mind where the return sits: indented inside the loop, it would leave the function after the first letter.

title: The grocer's prices
task:
Two functions for a shop. The prices are the ones Little Hours's grocer charges.

  • price_of(crop) returns 18 for "carrot" and for "tomato", 22 for "strawberry", 26 for "pumpkin", and 0 for anything the grocer does not sell. Use match.
  • can_buy(crop, coins) returns true only when the grocer sells the crop and the coins cover its price.
starter:
extends Node

func price_of(crop: String) -> int:
	match crop:
		_:
			return 0

func can_buy(crop: String, coins: int) -> bool:
	return false
solution:
extends Node

func price_of(crop: String) -> int:
	match crop:
		"carrot", "tomato":
			return 18
		"strawberry":
			return 22
		"pumpkin":
			return 26
		_:
			return 0

func can_buy(crop: String, coins: int) -> bool:
	var price := price_of(crop)
	return price > 0 and coins >= price

tests.label: can_buy("carrot", 18)  →  true: exactly enough
can_buy("turnip", 100)  →  false: not for sale at any price
price_of uses match

hints: Two patterns can share a branch: "carrot", "tomato":. New branches go above _:, which must stay last.
A price of 0 means "not sold". So can_buy is two conditions joined with and: the price is more than 0, and the coins are at least the price.
explain: Without the price > 0 half, a turnip would cost nothing and anybody could "buy" one: coins >= 0 is true for everyone. A default like 0 is convenient, and every caller has to remember what it means.

title: Saving up
task:
You have coins, you earn per_day more at the end of each day, and you want something that costs price. Finish days_to_afford(coins, per_day, price): how many days until you can pay.

  • If you can afford it already, the answer is 0.
  • If you cannot afford it and per_day is 0 or less, you never will: return -1. (Think about what a loop would do in that case.)

Use a while loop for the rest.

tests.label: days_to_afford(5, 10, 30)  →  3: 25 after two days is not enough
days_to_afford(30, 10, 30)  →  0: enough already
days_to_afford(50, 0, 10)  →  0: enough already, earning nothing
days_to_afford(0, 0, 10)  →  -1: never
days_to_afford(3, -2, 10)  →  -1: losing money every day
uses a while loop

hints: Inside the loop two things change each day: the coins go up by per_day and a day counter goes up by one. The loop runs while coins < price.
Do the two special cases before the loop, each with its own return: first "already enough", then "never". Only then is the loop certain to end.
explain: The two early returns are not decoration. Without the second, days_to_afford(0, 0, 10) adds nothing for ever – the line that should move the loop towards its end does not move it. Checking that a while can finish before starting it is a habit worth having. (You could also do this one with division; try it, and mind which way it rounds.)

title: A price with a default
task: Write price(count: int, each: int = 18) -> int, which returns what count items cost. When the caller does not say the price of one, it is 18. So price(3) is 54 and price(3, 20) is 60.

tests.label: price(3)  →  54: the default is 18
price(3, 20)  →  60: the caller's price wins

hints: Two parameters, and the second has = 18 after its type.
func price(count: int, each: int = 18) -> int: and return count * each.
explain: The default belongs to the parameter, not to the body: nothing inside the function checks whether each was given. When it is left out, Godot fills it in before the body runs.

title: Fix the bug: the answer that went to the screen
task: total(a, b) should hand back the sum of two numbers, and _ready() adds 1 to it. But Godot stops with an error. Look at what total actually does with its answer and fix it, so that total(2, 3) is 5 and the program prints 6.

tests.label: total(2, 3) hands back 5
prints exactly one line: 6

hints: print shows a value and gives back nothing. What does total(2, 3) + 1 make of that nothing?
Replace print(a + b) with return a + b. Printing is _ready()'s job.
explain: The original total printed 5 and returned null, so null + 1 was the error. With return the function answers the question it was asked, and _ready() chooses what to show. (Giving it -> int would have turned the mistake into an error in the editor, before you ran anything.)

title: Predict, then check
task:
Read the script, work out what _ready() leaves in each variable, and put your answers into the four guess variables. Then press Check; the checks run the real script and compare.

  • guess_count: the value of count at the end
  • guess_kept: the value of kept at the end
  • guess_list: the size() of list at the end
  • guess_total: the value of total at the end
starter:
extends Node

var guess_count = -1
var guess_kept = -1
var guess_list = -1
var guess_total = -1

var count := 1
var kept := 1
var list := [1]
var total := 0

func add_one(n: int) -> int:
	n += 1
	return n

func grow(items: Array) -> void:
	items.append(2)
	items.append(3)

func _ready() -> void:
	add_one(count)
	kept = add_one(kept)
	grow(list)
	var add := func(n): total += n
	add.call(10)
solution:
extends Node

var guess_count = 1
var guess_kept = 2
var guess_list = 3
var guess_total = 10

var count := 1
var kept := 1
var list := [1]
var total := 0

func add_one(n: int) -> int:
	n += 1
	return n

func grow(items: Array) -> void:
	items.append(2)
	items.append(3)

func _ready() -> void:
	add_one(count)
	kept = add_one(kept)
	grow(list)
	var add := func(n): total += n
	add.call(10)

tests.label: guess_count is what count ends as
guess_kept is what kept ends as
guess_list is the final size of list
guess_total is what total ends as

hints: A number is copied into a parameter; an array is not. And does anything keep the answer of the first add_one?
The lambda was written in _ready(), where total is a member variable of the script, not a local. Run the script and read each variable, if you are stuck: in the starter they do not change.
explain: Careful with the last one. total here is a variable of the script, not a local variable of _ready(), and a lambda can change a script's own variables, so it ends at 10. The copy-of-the-value rule from the chapter is about local variables: that was what made the earlier total stay at 0. count stays 1, because add_one's answer was thrown away; kept becomes 2 because its answer was stored; list holds three items because there was only ever one array.

title: A static helper that can say no
task: Inside the class Money, write a static func coins_back(paid: int, price: int) -> int that returns the change, or -1 when paid is less than price. Write the "not enough" case as a guard clause that returns first. It is called as Money.coins_back(20, 18).
starter:
extends Node

class Money:
	static func coins_back(paid: int, price: int) -> int:
		return 0

tests.label: Money.coins_back(20, 18)  →  2
paying exactly leaves no change: 0, not -1
not enough gives -1
it is a static function

hints: The case you are guarding against is paid < price. Return in it, and the line after is the ordinary rule.
if paid < price: then return -1, and after the if: return paid - price.
explain: Watch the boundary: < and not <=, because paying exactly the price is fine. Writing the exceptional case first leaves the last line to say the rule, with no else to indent under.

title: A function that makes functions
task: Write make_adder(n: int) -> Callable, which returns a lambda that adds n to whatever it is given. make_adder(5).call(3) is 8, and two adders made with different numbers must not interfere with each other.

tests.label: make_adder(5).call(3)  →  8
two adders in one expression do not interfere

hints: The lambda is made inside make_adder, so it can see n and keep its value.
return func(x): return x + n
explain: Each call to make_adder makes a new lambda holding its own copy of n, which is why they do not interfere – the "value at the moment it is made" rule working in your favour. A function that returns a function is how bind works, too.

title: Join two functions into one
task: Write compose(f: Callable, g: Callable) -> Callable: it returns a new Callable that, given x, runs f on it first and then g on the answer. compose(add_one, times_ten).call(2) is 30; reversed, it is 21. The two helpers are written for you.

tests.label: add one, then times ten: 2 becomes 30
the other way round: 2 becomes 21
a function can be composed with itself

hints: You are returning a lambda that takes x. Inside it, work from the inside out: first f.call(x).
return func(x): return g.call(f.call(x))
explain: add_one and times_ten are passed by their names without brackets, the method references from the chapter. compose never runs either of them: it builds something that will. When .call(2) arrives, f and g are still the two it was given.

title: Add up the basket
task: Finish total(prices) so that it returns the sum of all the numbers in the array. An empty array adds up to 0.
hints: Keep a running total in a variable that starts at 0, and add each item to it inside a for loop.
for p in prices: then sum += p, and return sum once the loop has finished – at the indent of the for, not inside it.

title: Ask the table
task:
The table of crops is given. Write two functions that read it:

  • grow_time(key: String) -> float returns the crop's "grow" value, or -1.0 when there is no such crop.
  • crop_names() -> Array returns the "name" of every crop, in the order of the table.

tests.label: grow_time("koi") is -1.0: there is no such crop

hints: One cell of the table is two lookups: CROPS[key]["grow"]. Guard it with CROPS.has(key), or reading a missing row stops the game.
For the names, start with an empty array, walk the table with for key in CROPS: and append each CROPS[key]["name"].
explain: The game reads this table the same way: _tick_farm() in Game.gd checks CROPS.has(crop) before it reads the grow time, so a plot that names a crop the table does not have is skipped and the game carries on.

title: Fix the bug: one plot or twelve?
task: This farm should have twelve separate plots. _ready() tills plot 0 and counts the tilled ones. Predict what it prints, then run it. Fix fresh_farm() so the script prints Tilled plots: 1. Leave till() and _ready() as they are.

tests.label: the farm still has 12 plots
plot 1 is still grass
till(5) tills plot 5
and leaves plot 6 alone

hints: How many times does fresh_plot() run? That is how many dictionaries exist.
Call it inside the loop: a.append(fresh_plot()). (a.append(plot.duplicate()) works too.)
explain: The broken version printed 12: one dictionary, appended twelve times, tilled once. The fix is the game's own _fresh_farm(), which you saw above.

title: Tally the harvest
task:
Write tally(items). It is given an array of names, such as a day's harvest in the order it was picked, and returns a dictionary from each name to how many times it appears. Keys are in the order they were first seen; an empty array gives an empty dictionary.

tally(["carrot", "tomato", "carrot"]) → { "carrot": 2, "tomato": 1 }

tests.label: tally([]) is an empty dictionary
keys are in the order first seen

hints: Start with an empty dictionary and walk the array. For each item, the new count is the old count plus one – and the old count of something not seen yet is 0.
counts[item] = counts.get(item, 0) + 1
explain: This is add_item() in a loop, and it is the most useful three lines in the chapter: any time you have a list and want to know "how many of each", it is this.

title: Top three, and leave my list alone
task: Write top_three(scores): it returns the three highest scores, highest first. With fewer than three scores it returns them all, still highest first. It must not change the array it was given – board has to be in the same order afterwards.
starter:
extends Node

var board := [40, 12, 77, 55]

func top_three(scores: Array) -> Array:
	scores.sort()
	return scores

func _ready() -> void:
	print(top_three(board))
	print(board)

tests.label: top_three([5, 9]) is [9, 5]
board is left exactly as it was

hints: The starter sorts the caller's own list, because an array passed to a function is shared, not copied. Work on a duplicate().
sort() puts the smallest first; reverse() turns that round; slice(0, 3) takes the first three, or fewer if there are fewer.
explain: A function that quietly reorders the list it was lent is a bug that shows up somewhere else, later. If a function changes what it is given, its name should say so; if its name does not, it should work on a copy.

title: What can I cook?
task:
A table of recipes – the game's own – maps each dish to the array of crops it needs. crops is your bag and dishes is what you have cooked. Write:

  • can_cook(dish: String) -> bool – true when the dish is in the table and the bag has at least one of every crop it needs.
  • cookable() -> Array – the names of the dishes you can cook now, in the order of the table.
  • cook(dish: String) -> bool – if the dish cannot be cooked, change nothing and return false. Otherwise take one of each crop out of the bag (erasing a key that reaches 0), add one to dishes[dish], and return true.

tests.label: can_cook("Harvest Pie") is false: no pumpkin
can_cook("Sunny Salad") is false: tomato but no sunflower
can_cook("Toast") is false: not in the table
cook("Roast Dinner") returns true
the bag is now { "carrot": 1 } – the tomato key is gone
and dishes is { "Roast Dinner": 1 }
now only Pancakes can be cooked
cook("Tomato Soup") returns false
and changes nothing

hints: RECIPES[dish] is an array, so you can walk it: for crop in RECIPES[dish]:. In can_cook, return false the moment one crop is missing, and true after the loop.
cookable() is a loop over the table that appends every dish for which can_cook(dish) is true.
cook() checks everything with can_cook() before it removes anything. Check and remove in the same loop and a Roast Dinner with no tomato would still eat the carrot.
explain: Check first, then change: the game's _cook() in Overlays.gd has the same two loops for the same reason. It makes one pass to be sure every ingredient is there, and only then a second that calls Game.add_item("crops", crop, -1) for each.

title: A class of your own
task: Give Crop an _init(t: String, d: int) that stores a title and a number of days, and make label() return a sentence in the form Carrot takes 3 days. Then change _ready() so that it makes a carrot that takes 3 days and prints its label.

tests.label: _init stores the title
and the days

hints: _init is a function inside the class. Its two lines copy the parameters into the object's variables: title = t and days = d.
For the sentence: "%s takes %d days" % [title, days], or title + " takes " + str(days) + " days".

title: One function different
task: Room describes itself as indoors. Write a class Garden that extends Room, so that Garden.new("Backyard").describe() returns Backyard (outdoors). Give it an _init(t: String) that passes the title up with super, and override one function only: is_outdoor(). Do not write a describe() for it.

tests.label: a Garden keeps its title
a Garden is a Room
a plain Room is still indoors
Garden does not rewrite describe()
tests.why: Garden inherits describe() from Room. Override is_outdoor() and let the inherited describe() call it.

hints: Start with class Garden extends Room:. Its _init(t: String) is one line, super(t).
Then func is_outdoor() -> bool: returning true. describe(), inherited from Room, calls it and gets the garden's answer.
explain: Room laid out the sentence and left one question open; Garden answered the question and nothing else. When you find yourself copying a whole function into a child to change one word of it, look for the question it could ask instead.

title: Fix the bug: the dog that never rests
task: Each morning a pet's new_day() should set its energy back to 5 and fed to false; for a dog it should also set walked to false. Predict what _ready() prints, then run it. Fix Dog so it prints [5, false, false], without copying any line out of Pet.

tests.label: Dog's new_day() calls Pet's with super.new_day()
tests.why: Do not copy Pet's lines into Dog: call super.new_day().

hints: It prints [1, true, false]. Dog's new_day() replaced Pet's, so the two lines in Pet never ran.
Make the first line of Dog's new_day() a call to the original: super.new_day().
explain: An override replaces; it does not add. Whenever the parent's version did something that still has to happen, the child's version calls super. It is the first line of the game's LampRun._ready() for exactly this reason.

title: A class with no objects
task:
Write two static functions in Clock, so that they can be called as Clock.fraction(t) and Clock.phase(t) without making a clock. t is seconds into the day.

  • fraction(t: float) -> float – t divided by DAY_LENGTH, kept between 0.0 and 1.0.
  • phase(t: float) -> String – "Morning" while the fraction is below 0.2, "Daytime" below 0.55, "Evening" below 0.75, and "Night" after that.

tests.label: Clock.fraction(999.0) is 1.0: it never goes past the end of the day
Clock.fraction(-5.0) is 0.0
phase() is a static func
tests.why: Write static func, so it can be called on the class.

hints: Both start with static func and sit inside the class, indented under it. A static function can use the class's constants and its other static functions.
clampf(value, low, high) keeps a number between two limits. phase() is a ladder of ifs on fraction(t), lowest limit first.
explain: The numbers are the game's (the clock). There the two functions are ordinary ones on the Game autoload and read its own clock_t. Making them static and passing t in means you can ask about any moment, not only now, and that makes them easy to test.

title: A resident with a look
task:
PaperDoll and Sketch are two ways to draw a person. Finish Resident, which has a look and can change it:

  • a new resident starts with a PaperDoll in its look variable;
  • use_sketch(on: bool) replaces the look with a new Sketch when on is true, or a new PaperDoll when it is false;
  • is_sketch() -> bool says which it has;
  • walk(dir: String) -> String returns the title, then : , then whatever the look's show(dir) returns.

Resident must not extend either look.

tests.label: a new resident starts as a paper doll
after _ready(), you are a sketch
use_sketch(false) changes you back
and look holds a PaperDoll object again
Resident does not extend a look
tests.why: A resident has a look; it is not one.

hints: Set the first look in _init: look = PaperDoll.new().
is_sketch() is one line with is: return look is Sketch.
walk() passes the work on: return title + ": " + look.show(dir). It never asks which kind of look it has.
explain: This is Player.gd in miniature: use_sketch() is its _rebuild_avatar(), and walk() is every place it tells _avatar to face along the way it is moving, without asking which avatar that is. The one function that needs to know the kind, is_sketch(), asks with is.

title: Predict, then check: the order
task: Read the script, work out the order of the four lines it prints, and put them in guess, one string per line, in the order they appear. Then check.

tests.label: four lines
the variable's starting value is worked out before _init
_ready runs after _init, and its calls in order
and that is what the script prints

hints: Variables get their starting value first. Then the object is built. Then the node is ready.
The order is variable, init, ready, sub.
explain: Running it is a good way to settle a doubt about order: put a print in each function and look. The starting value of a variable is part of making the object, so it comes before _init.

title: Fix the bug: the slow machine
task: step(delta) is called once a frame, and it should move x at 100 units a second. Tested on a fast machine, one second is sixty frames of 1/60; on a slow one, thirty frames of 1/30. The checks run both: it should be at 100 after either. Fix step without touching the checks.

tests.label: a second of 60 frames moves 100
a second of 30 frames moves 100 too
and so does 144
uses delta
tests.why: The step has to depend on how long the frame was.

hints: The step is a constant, so it is the same however long the frame was. What should it depend on?
x += SPEED * delta
explain: The original had the frame rate baked in: it was right at 60 and wrong anywhere else, the sort of bug that is invisible on the machine you wrote it on. SPEED * delta is "units a second, times a part of a second".

title: A cooldown
task: Write a little cooldown. tick(delta) is called every frame. When ready_in is above zero it counts down by delta (and never goes below 0). use() returns false while the cooldown is running; when it is not, it returns true and sets ready_in to COOLDOWN (1.5 seconds).
starter:
extends Node

const COOLDOWN := 1.5

var ready_in := 0.0

func tick(delta: float) -> void:
	pass

func use() -> bool:
	return true

tests.label: the first use works
the second, straight after, does not
the cooldown is 1.5 seconds
tick(0.5) twice: 0.5 left
it never goes below 0
and it can be used again

hints: Two jobs: tick counts down and stops at zero; use asks "is it still running?" first.
ready_in = maxf(ready_in - delta, 0.0) in tick. In use: if ready_in > 0.0 return false; otherwise set it and return true.
explain: The countdown is the timer from the chapter turned upside down: count down to 0 and stop, rather than up to a limit. maxf is the "never below" in one go. A guard clause in use deals with the busy case first.

title: Ready order of a tree
task: Write enter_order(node: Dictionary, out: Array) -> void: it fills out with the names in the order _enter_tree would run, parents before children, each parent's children in the order they are listed. Each node is {"name": ..., "kids": [...]}. The scene, a working ready_order for comparison, and two helpers that run each walk on the scene are written for you.

tests.label: Main, Room, Chair, Lamp, Hud
the same five nodes as ready_order
and ready_order still goes children first

hints: It is ready_order with the out.append(...) line before the loop instead of after it.
out.append(node["name"]), then the for that calls enter_order(kid, out).
explain: One line moved, and the order flips: parents before children is the walk down (_enter_tree); children before parents is the walk back up (_ready).

title: Answer the door
task: The signal and the listener are written; nothing joins them. In _ready(), connect _greet to door_opened, then emit the signal twice – once for "Wren" and once for "Bo" – so the output is Welcome, Wren then Welcome, Bo. Do not call _greet yourself.
solution:
extends Node

signal door_opened(who: String)

func _ready() -> void:
	door_opened.connect(_greet)
	door_opened.emit("Wren")
	door_opened.emit("Bo")

func _greet(who: String) -> void:
	print("Welcome, ", who)

tests.label: _greet is connected to door_opened
tests.why: door_opened.connect(_greet) – the name, without brackets.

tests.label: the greetings come from emitting the signal
tests.why: Emit the signal: door_opened.emit("Wren")

hints: Connect first. A connection only hears what is emitted after it is made.
Three lines: door_opened.connect(_greet), then door_opened.emit("Wren") and the same for Bo.

title: Fix the bug: the empty basket
task: This should record three harvests – 3 beans, then 2 more beans, then 1 squash – and print { "beans": 5, "squash": 1 }. Instead it stops with an error. There are two mistakes, both in _ready(); fix one and you will meet the other. Leave _on_harvested alone.
starter:
extends Node

signal harvested(crop: String, amount: int)

var basket := {}

func _ready() -> void:
	harvested.connect(_on_harvested())
	harvested.emit("beans")
	harvested.emit("beans", 2)
	harvested.emit("squash", 1)
	print(basket)

func _on_harvested(crop: String, amount: int) -> void:
	basket[crop] = basket.get(crop, 0) + amount
solution:
extends Node

signal harvested(crop: String, amount: int)

var basket := {}

func _ready() -> void:
	harvested.connect(_on_harvested)
	harvested.emit("beans", 3)
	harvested.emit("beans", 2)
	harvested.emit("squash", 1)
	print(basket)

func _on_harvested(crop: String, amount: int) -> void:
	basket[crop] = basket.get(crop, 0) + amount

tests.label: five beans in the basket
one squash in the basket

hints: Look at what is handed to connect. Is it a function, or the result of calling one?
The signal declares two parameters and the listener takes two. Does every emit send two?
explain: _on_harvested() with brackets tries to call the function on the spot, with no arguments. Once that is fixed, harvested.emit("beans") sends one value to a function that needs two. Both are the same kind of mistake: the signal's declaration, every emit and every listener have to agree on what is carried.

title: One function, three buttons
task: Three buttons, one handler. In _ready(), connect each button's pressed signal to _on_menu so that play_button sends "play", options_button sends "options" and quit_button sends "quit". Do not write any new functions. click_all() is there for the checks to press them with.

tests.label: _ready() clicks options and prints Opening options
clicking play, options, quit opens them in that order
uses bind to tell the buttons apart
tests.why: pressed carries nothing, so the name has to be bound to each connection.

hints: pressed sends no values and _on_menu needs one. bind fills it in.
play_button.pressed.connect(_on_menu.bind("play")), and two more like it.
explain: With real Button nodes this is how a menu, an inventory grid or a row of save slots is wired: one function, and each connection carrying the one thing that differs. If the buttons were in an Array you could connect them in a loop, binding the loop variable.

title: A mute switch
task: Every coin plays a chime because _play_chime is connected to coin_collected. Finish set_muted(on): muting must disconnect the chime, and un-muting must connect it again. It has to be safe to call with the same value twice in a row – muting when already muted, or un-muting when already connected, must do nothing and must not be an error. collect(times) is there for the checks.

tests.label: two coins, two chimes
muted: three more coins and still 2 chimes
muting again is harmless
un-muted: the next coin chimes
un-muting again is harmless – one chime per coin, no error
muted follows what was asked
muting disconnects the listener
tests.why: The exercise is to stop listening, not to ignore what is heard.

hints: Ask before you act: coin_collected.is_connected(_play_chime) tells you whether there is anything to disconnect, or whether connecting would be a second connection.
Two cases do something: on and connected → disconnect; not on and not connected → connect. The other two cases do nothing.
explain: An if muted: return at the top of _play_chime would also silence it, and for one listener that is fine. Disconnecting is the better habit when the listener is expensive or there are many: a signal with nobody connected does no work at all.

title: Predict, then check: who goes first?
task: Do not run this in your head for long – commit to an answer. The script appends five letters to seen as it runs. Replace the question marks in guess with the letters in the order you think they are appended, then press Check. Change nothing else.
starter:
extends Node

signal door_opened

var seen: Array = []
var guess := ["?", "?", "?", "?", "?"]

func _ready() -> void:
	seen.append("A")
	wait_at_door()
	seen.append("B")
	door_opened.emit()
	seen.append("C")

func wait_at_door() -> void:
	seen.append("D")
	await door_opened
	seen.append("E")
solution:
extends Node

signal door_opened

var seen: Array = []
var guess := ["A", "D", "B", "E", "C"]

func _ready() -> void:
	seen.append("A")
	wait_at_door()
	seen.append("B")
	door_opened.emit()
	seen.append("C")

func wait_at_door() -> void:
	seen.append("D")
	await door_opened
	seen.append("E")

tests.label: the script still appends five letters
first letter
second letter
third letter
fourth letter
fifth letter

hints: Calling wait_at_door() runs it straight away, as far as its await. Then where does control go?
The paused function wakes inside door_opened.emit() – before the line after the emit.
explain: A, D, B, E, C. The call runs wait_at_door() until its await (A, then D), which hands control back to _ready() (B). The emit wakes the waiting function, which runs to its end (E) before emit returns, and only then does _ready() reach its last line (C). If you want to see it, add print(seen) at the end of _ready().

title: Three knocks
task: Somebody knocks three times, a second apart, and each knock has a loudness. Write count_knocks(times) so that it waits for the knocked signal that many times, adds up the loudness each one carries, and returns the total. With the three timers in _ready() the output must be Three knocks, total loudness 8.
solution:
extends Node

signal knocked(loudness: int)

func _ready() -> void:
	get_tree().create_timer(1.0).timeout.connect(func() -> void: knocked.emit(2))
	get_tree().create_timer(2.0).timeout.connect(func() -> void: knocked.emit(5))
	get_tree().create_timer(3.0).timeout.connect(func() -> void: knocked.emit(1))
	var total: int = await count_knocks(3)
	print("Three knocks, total loudness ", total)

func count_knocks(times: int) -> int:
	var total := 0
	for i in times:
		var loudness: int = await knocked
		total += loudness
	return total

tests.label: count_knocks() waits for the knocked signal
tests.why: Use await knocked – it gives you the loudness that knock carried.

tests.label: waits in a loop, as many times as asked
tests.why: times could be any number: loop, and await once each time round.

hints: await knocked is an expression: it pauses, and when the signal arrives it gives back the one value the signal carried.
An await can sit inside a loop. Each time round, the function pauses again until the next knock.
for i in times: then total += await knocked, and return total after the loop.
explain: The function holds its place in a loop across three seconds and three separate events, and its local variable total survives each pause. Doing this with connect would need a counter and a total kept as script variables, a listener, and a disconnect at the end. This is the shape of every "wait for the player to do this three times" in a tutorial.

title: A torch
task: The beam is drawn all the time. Make it shine only while ui_accept (Space) is held down: every frame, set the node's visible property to whether the action is pressed.

tests.label: with nothing held, the torch is off
while ui_accept is held, it is on
and it goes off again when the key is let go

hints: Input.is_action_pressed("ui_accept") is already a true or false. It can be assigned straight to visible.
visible = Input.is_action_pressed("ui_accept")

title: Fix the bug: the eager counter
task: This should count how many times Space (ui_accept) has been pressed. Play it and press once: the number jumps by five or ten. Fix it so one press counts one, however long the key is held.

tests.label: holding the key for half a second counts one press
a quick tap counts one more
and nothing is counted while the key is up

hints: The game asks its question sixty times a second. For how many of those frames is your finger on the key?
One word is missing from the name of the function: is_action_just_pressed.
explain: is_action_pressed is true on every frame the key is down, and a quick press lasts several. is_action_just_pressed is true on the first of them only. Whenever something happens "too many times" on one press, this is the first place to look.

title: Who gets the tap?
task: Three buttons are on screen, each a name and a rectangle. Finish who_gets(tap): it returns the name of the button the tap is on, or "world" if it is on none. Two of the buttons overlap. The one later in the list was added later and is drawn on top, so it must win – as it does in Godot.
starter:
extends Node

var buttons := [
	{"name": "menu", "rect": Rect2(250, 4, 64, 24)},
	{"name": "bag", "rect": Rect2(4, 150, 48, 24)},
	{"name": "map", "rect": Rect2(30, 150, 48, 24)},
]

func who_gets(tap: Vector2) -> String:
	return "world"

tests.label: who_gets(Vector2(10, 160))  →  "bag" (the part of the bag the map does not cover)
who_gets(Vector2(40, 160))  →  "map" (both are here; the later one is on top)

hints: rect.has_point(tap) says whether a Rect2 contains a point.
Going through the list forwards finds the bag before the map. Go through it backwards: for i in range(buttons.size() - 1, -1, -1):
explain: This is the middle stop of the event queue in miniature. Controls later in the tree are drawn over earlier ones and are offered a click first; the first to contain it consumes it; and what nobody contains falls through to _unhandled_input – the "world" at the bottom.

title: The tap that came twice
task: count_presses(events) should say how many times the player pressed. It counts every event whose "pressed" is true, so one tap on a phone counts as two: the touch, and the mouse click Godot makes from it. Make it skip the copies – a "mouse" event whose "device" is DEVICE_ID_EMULATION – while still counting clicks from a real mouse.

tests.label: one tap on a phone is one press
one click of a real mouse is one press
tap, click, tap is three presses
no events, no presses

hints: Do not drop every mouse event: a desktop player has nothing else. The copy is the one whose device is DEVICE_ID_EMULATION.
First thing in the loop: if event["type"] == "mouse" and event["device"] == DEVICE_ID_EMULATION: continue
explain: The solution gives the test a name, is_touch_copy, as the game does. With real events the same check is event is InputEventMouse and event.device == InputEvent.DEVICE_ID_EMULATION. Skipping the copy and keeping the touch, not the other way round, means the code still sees each finger's index.

title: Rebind without a clash
task:
A settings screen lets the player change a key. On this model of the Input Map, write two functions.

  • action_using(key) returns the name of the action that has key in its list, or "" if none does.
  • rebind(action, old_key, new_key) replaces old_key with new_key in that action's list, in the same place, and returns true. It changes nothing and returns false if there is no such action, if old_key is not one of its keys, or if new_key is already used by any action.

tests.label: rebind("jump", "Space", "W") works and returns true
jump is now on W
and Space is free
rebinding interact to A is refused: move_left has A
and interact is unchanged
there is no action called fly
Q is not one of move_left's keys
rebind("move_left", "Left", "J") returns true
and J took Left's place, after A

hints: action_using is a loop over the dictionary's keys with key in input_map[action] inside – the first section of the chapter has nearly this.
In rebind, do all three refusals before changing anything. keys.find(old_key) gives the position, or -1.
Arrays are shared, not copied (Chapter G): var keys: Array = input_map[action] then keys[at] = new_key changes the list inside the dictionary.
explain: On the real thing the same job is InputMap.action_erase_event(action, old_event) followed by InputMap.action_add_event(action, new_event), with the clash check done by looping over InputMap.get_actions() and asking InputMap.action_has_event(). Changes made that way last until the game closes, so a settings screen also saves them (Chapter S) and applies them again at the start.

title: Double tap to dash
task: Make the square dash on a double tap of ui_accept: two presses no more than WINDOW seconds apart. A dash adds DASH to position.x and 1 to dashes. A single press does nothing, and neither do two slow ones. A dash uses up both of its presses: a third quick press is the first half of a new pair, not another dash.

tests.label: one press alone does nothing
a second press an eighth of a second later is a dash
and the square has moved 60 pixels right
a third quick press starts a new pair – no dash yet
the fourth completes it
waiting a second changes nothing
a press after the wait is a first press again
half a second goes by
a press that late is too slow to be a double: still two dashes' worth of distance

hints: Input only knows about now. "How long ago was the last press?" is a variable you keep: add delta to it every frame and set it to 0 on a press.
On each is_action_just_pressed: if the timer is within WINDOW, dash; otherwise this press is the first of a pair, so restart the timer.
After a dash, set the timer to something large, so the next press cannot pair with the one that has been used.
explain: This is the pattern behind every input that is about time – double taps, holding to charge, a short hop against a long jump: poll for the moment, and keep a clock of your own for everything else. Counting in seconds with delta, not in frames, is what makes the window the same length on every screen (Chapter T).

title: Where is the hat?
task:
A parent that is not turned or scaled. Finish both functions:

  • global_of(parent_pos, local) – where a child with that local position is in the world
  • local_of(parent_pos, global) – the local position a child needs to be at that place in the world

tests.label: there and back again gives the local position you started with

hints: A local position is an arrow that starts at the parent.
One is an addition and the other is the subtraction that undoes it.
explain: These are to_global() and to_local() for the simplest possible parent. With rotation and scale the sums grow, but the idea – add the parent on the way out, take it off on the way in – does not change.

title: Predict, then check
task: No code to write: four predictions. Replace each 0.0 (and the Vector2.ZERO) with the value you expect from the expression in its comment. Work them out in your head or on paper first; then press Run, which prints the real answers, and compare.

tests.label: guess_length is the length of (6, 8)
guess_up_y is the y after going 20 px up
guess_down_degrees is the angle of DOWN, in degrees
guess_halfway is the midpoint

hints: (6, 8) is a 3-4-5 triangle, doubled.
Up the screen is less y, and angles are measured clockwise from "right".
explain: If the second or third surprised you, that is the y-down rule. It is worth being surprised by it here and not at midnight, in a game, with a character that jumps into the floor.

title: Fix the bug: faster on the diagonal
task: step() returns how far a character moves in one frame, given which keys are held. A tester reports that running diagonally is quicker than running straight. Fix it, so that any combination of keys moves at exactly SPEED – and no keys at all still gives Vector2.ZERO.

tests.label: right alone: 50 px in half a second
down alone: 50 px, and down is +y
right and down together: still 50 px
…shared equally between x and y
no keys: no movement

hints: Run it. What is the length of (1, 1)?
The direction must be 1 long before it is multiplied by the speed: dir.normalized().
explain: (1, 1) is about 1.414 long, so the diagonal ran at 141% speed. Normalising costs nothing when the vector is already 1 long, and Vector2.ZERO.normalized() is still zero, so it is safe to do always.

title: Sort by the feet
task:
Each thing in a scene is a Dictionary with a "name", the "centre" of its picture and the picture's "height" – centred sprites, as Godot makes them by default. Write:

  • foot_y(thing) -> float – the y of the bottom edge of the picture
  • draw_order(things) -> Array – the names, in the order to paint them: furthest back (smallest foot) first

Sorting by centre.y gives the wrong answer for the scene below; that is the point.

tests.label: the tree's foot is at y = 120
your feet are at y = 118
you are painted first: you are standing just behind the tree
a cat (foot 85) is behind a tall lamp (foot 100)
the scene itself is left in its own order

hints: A centred picture reaches half its height below its centre.
Sort a duplicate() of the list with sort_custom(func(a, b): return foot_y(a) < foot_y(b)), then collect the names.
explain: This is Little Hours's rule exactly: centre.y plus the distance down to the foot. The game writes the result into each sprite's z_index and lets Godot do the sorting.

title: Keep the camera in the room
task: Write camera_centre(target, view, room): the point a camera should centre on. It is target, except that the view (a Vector2 size) must never show anything outside the room, which runs from (0, 0) to room. One more case: if the room is smaller than the view along an axis, centre on the middle of the room on that axis.

tests.label: in the middle of the room the camera is on the target
in the top-left corner it stops half a view in: (160, 90)
in the bottom-right corner: (480, 270)
each axis is clamped on its own
a room only 200 wide: x is the room's middle, y still follows

hints: The centre must stay half a view from each edge: between view.x / 2 and room.x - view.x / 2. That is a clampf.
When the room is narrower than the view those two limits cross over, which is why the small room needs an if of its own, per axis.
explain: The small-room case is not a curiosity: a small shop on a big phone is exactly it. Little Hours deals with it from the other end – on a phone, Game.apply_room() never lets a room be smaller than what the camera shows.

title: A moon, and a moon's moon
task:
Your node is a planet in the middle of the view, at (160, 90). Give it a moon that circles it and a satellite that circles the moon: three levels of local space.

  • angle grows by TURN radians a second.
  • moon_local() – the moon's position relative to the planet: ORBIT pixels away, turned by angle. At angle 0 it is directly to the right.
  • satellite_local() – the satellite's position relative to the moon: SAT_ORBIT pixels away, turned by three times angle.
  • satellite_global() – where the satellite is on the screen.

Then draw both in _draw(). Remember that this node draws in its own local space, and that a drawing is kept until you ask for a new one.

tests.label: at the start the moon is 50 px to the right of the planet
after one second the angle is a quarter turn
a quarter turn puts the moon BELOW the planet: (0, 50)
the satellite has gone three quarters round the moon: (0, -12)
on the screen the satellite is at (160, 128)
a second later it is at (98, 90)
asks for a new drawing with queue_redraw()
tests.why: Without it _draw() runs once and nothing appears to move.

hints: Vector2(ORBIT, 0).rotated(angle) is an arrow ORBIT long, turned by angle.
Global is the sum of every local on the way up: the planet's position, plus the moon's local position, plus the satellite's.
In _draw() you are already in the planet's space, so the moon goes at moon_local() and the satellite at moon_local() + satellite_local() – with no position added.
explain: The moon swings down first, because a positive angle is clockwise when y points down. In Godot you would not write any of the sums: make the moon a child of the planet and the satellite a child of the moon, turn each parent, and read global_position. The engine is doing this addition, all the way up the tree, for every node, every frame.

title: Which one was tapped?
task: Write tapped(p, rects): the index of the first rectangle in the list rects that contains the point p, or -1 if none does. Use Rect2.has_point().

tests.label: a tap on the first button gives 0
a tap on the second gives 1
a tap on the third gives 2
where the second and third overlap, the first of them wins: 1
a tap on nothing gives -1
an empty list gives -1

hints: You need the index, so loop over numbers: for i in rects.size():.
Inside the loop: if rects[i].has_point(p): return i. After it: return -1.
explain: Returning from inside the loop is what makes "the first" win. A game that draws later things on top wants the last match instead – walk the list backwards, or do as Little Hours does and keep the match with the highest z_index.

title: Close enough to touch
task: Write overlapping(a, ra, b, rb): true when a circle of radius ra centred on a overlaps a circle of radius rb centred on b. Circles that only just touch – exactly as far apart as their radii added together – do not count.

tests.label: 8 apart, radii 5 and 5: overlapping
20 apart, radii 5 and 5: not
(3, 4) apart is 5; radii 2 and 4: overlapping
(6, 8) apart is exactly 10; radii 5 and 5: only touching
the same place always overlaps

hints: How far apart are the centres? a.distance_to(b).
Compare that with ra + rb, using <.

title: Fix the bug: the walker that shivers
task: This walker heads for target at SPEED, a tenth of a second per step. Run it: it gets close and then hops back and forth across the target for ever. Fix step() so that it lands exactly on the target and stays there, without changing how fast it walks on the way.

tests.label: on the way it still walks 9 pixels a step: 9, 18, 27 … 99
once it has had time to get there, pos is exactly the target
three steps later it has not moved
nor after one more

hints: Print the positions and look at the two numbers either side of 100. How long is one step?
The step has to be shortened when the target is nearer than a full step. Vector2.move_toward(to, step) does exactly that.
explain: A step is 9 pixels and the target is at 100, so the walker goes 99, 108, 99, 108. Any fix that checks "would this step pass the target?" works; move_toward is that check with a name. The other common cure is to stop when "near enough" – Little Hours calls its near-enough ARRIVE_EPS, 2.5 pixels – which is fine as long as near enough is bigger than half a step.

title: Layers and masks, as numbers
task:
Three small functions about collision layers, which are numbered from 1:

  • bit(layer_number) – the value of that layer's bit: 1 for layer 1, 2 for layer 2, 4 for layer 3, 8 for layer 4…
  • mask_of(layers) – the single integer with the bit of every layer number in the list set: mask_of([1, 3]) is 5
  • notices(mask, other_layers) – true when mask shares at least one bit with other_layers, the other object's collision_layer value

tests.label: an empty list is a mask of 0: looks for nothing
a mask of walls and coins notices a coin
a mask of walls alone does not
an object in two layers is noticed through either
a mask of 0 notices nothing

hints: 1 << n is 1 moved n places to the left: 1, 2, 4, 8. Layer 1 needs zero moves.
Join bits with | (or |= in a loop, starting from 0). Find shared bits with &, and put it in brackets before comparing: (mask & other_layers) != 0.
explain: This is the whole of the layer system: 32 yes-or-no answers packed into one integer, and one & to compare two of them. In a project you would call set_collision_mask_value(3, true) and never see the numbers, but now a collision_mask = 5 in a scene file reads as "layers 1 and 3".

title: The foot of the furniture
task:
Little Hours's rule for what blocks you. Given the rectangle a sprite is drawn in, write:

  • foot_box(sprite) – the blocking box: FOOT_W_FRAC of the sprite's width, centred left to right, and FOOT_H_FRAC of its height, sitting on the sprite's bottom edge
  • can_stand(p, sprite) – true when the point p is not inside that box

tests.label: the sofa's foot is 164 wide (82% of 200)
…and 50 high (half of 100)
it starts at x = 118, leaving 18 px clear each side
its bottom edge is the sprite's bottom edge, y = 300
a 50 x 80 lamp at the origin: the foot starts at y = 40
you can stand behind the sofa, in the top half of its picture
you cannot stand in its base
you can stand in the 18 px at its side

hints: Work out the foot's width and height first: sprite.size.x * FOOT_W_FRAC and sprite.size.y * FOOT_H_FRAC.
Its left edge is the sprite's left edge plus half of the width left over; its top is sprite.end.y minus the foot's height.
can_stand is not foot_box(sprite).has_point(p).
explain: Compare your foot_box with the game's solids() above: the same four numbers in the same order. Blocking only the foot is what lets a character walk "behind" furniture in a flat picture.

title: Take the wheel
task:
Drive the walker with the arrow keys, with weight, in a room with a wall in it. blocked() is written for you: it is true inside the wall and outside the floor.

  • Each frame the velocity you want is the direction of the keys (ui_left, ui_right, ui_up, ui_down) times SPEED.
  • vel does not jump to it: it moves towards it by ACCEL * delta each frame, so starting and stopping both take a fifth of a second.
  • Move by vel * delta, one axis at a time, so they slide along the wall.
  • When an axis is refused, set that part of vel to 0 – or they store up speed while pushing at the wall.

tests.label: a tenth of a second after pressing right, vel.x is 60: half speed
it tops out at SPEED

tests.expr: not blocked(pos) and pos.x > 135.0 and pos.x <= 142.0
tests.label: held against the wall, they stop at its face
…and are not storing up speed: vel.x is far below SPEED
right and down together: they slide down the wall
let go, and they are still moving a moment later
…and then at rest

hints: The first two lines: var want := Input.get_vector("ui_left", "ui_right", "ui_up", "ui_down") * SPEED, then vel = vel.move_toward(want, ACCEL * delta).
This frame's step is vel * delta. Test Vector2(pos.x + step.x, pos.y): if it is blocked, vel.x = 0.0; otherwise pos.x += step.x.
Then the same for y, testing Vector2(pos.x, pos.y + step.y).
explain: Tap a key and they glide a little; hold one into the wall and they stop without stored-up speed; hold two and they slide. This is how Little Hours moves when you hold a key: _vel.move_toward(want, rate * delta), then the per-axis slide – with a harder rate for braking than for speeding up, which you can try by using a bigger number when want is shorter than vel.

title: Which frame is showing?
task: Finish frame_at(t, fps, count): the number of the frame showing t seconds into a looping animation of count frames played at fps frames a second. Frames are numbered from 0.

tests.label: frame_at(0.5, 8.0, 4) has looped back to 0
frame_at(1.25, 2.0, 6) is the int 2

hints: t * fps is how many frames have gone by, as a float. int() drops the fraction.
Wrap it with % count: int(t * fps) % count.

title: Cut the frame out
task:
A sheet has hframes columns of frames, each w pixels wide and h tall, numbered left to right and then down. Write frame_region(frame, hframes, w, h) to return the Rect2 of pixels for a frame – what you would give to region_rect.

The checks use the sheet of the game's paper doll: 3 columns of 48 × 96 frames.

tests.label: frame 4 of a 3-column sheet is column 1, row 1
frame 11 is the last: column 2, row 3

hints: The column is what is left over after taking out whole rows: frame % hframes.
The row is how many whole rows fit: frame / hframes, with both sides int so the division drops the remainder.
explain: A Sprite2D with hframes and vframes set does this for you when you assign frame. Doing it by hand is what lets the game give one rectangle to five stacked sprites at once.

title: Predict: arrive, or only approach?
task:
Predict, then check. Read the two functions below without running anything, and type your answers into the two variables at the top:

  • guess_calls – how many times does count_calls() go round its loop before a equals 10.0?
  • guess_b – what does b_after_four() return?

Then press Check. If you are wrong, add a print inside the loop and find out why.
starter:
extends Node

var guess_calls := -1      # your prediction
var guess_b := -1.0        # your prediction

func count_calls() -> int:
	var a := 0.0
	var calls := 0
	while a != 10.0:
		a = move_toward(a, 10.0, 3.0)
		calls += 1
	return calls

func b_after_four() -> float:
	var b := 0.0
	for i in 4:
		b = lerpf(b, 10.0, 0.5)
	return b
solution:
extends Node

var guess_calls := 4       # 3, 6, 9, then 10: the last step is cut short
var guess_b := 9.375       # 5, 7.5, 8.75, 9.375: half of what is left, each time

func count_calls() -> int:
	var a := 0.0
	var calls := 0
	while a != 10.0:
		a = move_toward(a, 10.0, 3.0)
		calls += 1
	return calls

func b_after_four() -> float:
	var b := 0.0
	for i in 4:
		b = lerpf(b, 10.0, 0.5)
	return b

tests.label: guess_calls is the number of calls move_toward needs
guess_b is what four lerps leave in b

hints: move_toward(a, 10.0, 3.0) adds 3, but never goes past 10. Write down a after each call.
lerpf(b, 10.0, 0.5) moves b half of the way that is left: 5, then half of the remaining 5, and so on.
explain: move_toward goes 3, 6, 9 and then exactly 10: it never overshoots, which is why a loop that waits for a == 10.0 is safe with it. The lerp halves the gap every time – 5, 7.5, 8.75, 9.375 – and a gap that keeps halving is not a thing to wait on. When you need to know that something has arrived, use move_toward, or compare with a small distance instead of ==.

title: Fix the bug: twice as fast on a fast screen
task:
This four-square spinner is meant to step FPS times a second – four steps, one whole turn, every second. Press Play: it is a blur. It moves on once for every frame the screen draws, so its speed depends on the screen.

Fix it so that frame comes from time. Keep the name frame and keep FPS and FRAMES; add whatever else you need.

tests.label: after 0.75 s on a fast screen (24 short frames), frame is 3
after another 0.75 s on a slower screen (12 longer frames), frame is 2
and half a second after that it is 0

hints: The function is handed delta and ignores it. Add a variable that counts seconds: t += delta.
Then the frame is the chapter's one-liner: frame = int(t * FPS) % FRAMES.
explain: The checks run the same script at two frame rates and expect the same animation, which is the only real test of "does it use delta". Counting calls to _process is counting screen refreshes, and no two devices agree on those (Chapter T has more on why counting frames is a bug).

title: A tween by hand
task:
Write the heart of a tween. tween_at(from, to, duration, elapsed) returns the value of a property elapsed seconds into a tween from from to to lasting duration seconds, eased out with ease_out.

Before the tween starts (a negative elapsed) it must return from, and after it ends it must return to – exactly, however late it is asked. The version below does neither, and is not eased.

tests.label: half-way through the time, an ease-out is three quarters of the way there
long after the end it is still exactly at the target
before the start it has not moved
it works downwards too: 50 to 10, half-way through, is 20

hints: Three stages: time into a share (elapsed / duration), the share bent by the curve, the bent share into a value with lerpf.
Clamp the share before easing it: clampf(elapsed / duration, 0.0, 1.0). An ease is only defined from 0 to 1.
explain: The clamp matters more than it looks. ease_out(2.5) is −1.25: without it, a tween asked for its value late would fling the property backwards past where it started. A real Tween does this clamping for you and finishes by writing the final value itself.

title: One step after another
task:
Tween steps chain: each starts where the one before ended. Write chain_at(start, steps, t), the value t seconds into a chain of plain, uneased steps.

steps is an Array of [to, duration] pairs. The dog's bounce in the game is nearly [[-16.0, 0.125], [0.0, 0.25]] from a start of 0.0: up to −16 in an eighth of a second, back to 0 in a quarter. After the last step the value stays at the last to; with no steps at all it is start. A step whose to equals the value it starts from is a wait, and needs no special code.

tests.label: the bounce at 0 s: on the floor
half-way through the first step: −8
the moment the first step ends: −16
half-way through the second step: back to −8
long after the end: 0
no steps: the start value
a step that goes nowhere is a wait
and the step after the wait starts when it ends

hints: Walk the steps in order, carrying two things: the value the current step starts from, and how much time is left to spend.
If the time left is less than this step's duration, the answer is inside this step: lerpf(from, to, t / duration). Otherwise take the duration off the time, make from this step's to, and go on.
If the loop ends without returning, every step is over: return the last from.
explain: This is what a Tween keeps track of between frames: which step it is in and how far through. Put ease_out from the last exercise round t / duration and each step eases; give each step its own curve and you have set_trans.

title: Centre it on the node
task:
Press Play. The card hangs down and to the right of the white dot, because a Rect2 is given by its top-left corner and the script puts that corner on the origin.

Fix centred(size) so that it returns a rectangle of that size whose centre is the origin. Then change the numbers in position and play again: the card and the dot move together, and the drawing code has not changed.

tests.label: the centre of centred(Vector2(7, 7)) is the origin
_draw() runs without an error

hints: The top-left corner has to be half the size up and to the left of the origin.
Rect2(-size / 2.0, size) – a Rect2 can be made from a position and a size, both Vector2s.
explain: Where you put the origin is a decision. A bar is easiest to place by its centre; a character is best drawn upwards from the feet, so that the feet are what position means (Chapter N did exactly that).

title: A face from five calls
task:
A sandbox for the calls in the table. The face is drawn; give it the rest:

  • two eyes, with draw_circle;
  • a smile, with draw_arc – the angles from 0.5 to PI - 0.5 sweep through straight down, which is the bottom of a circle;
  • the brim of a hat, or an eyebrow, with draw_line.

The positions and sizes are yours to choose. The checks only ask that each call is used and that the script runs.
solution:
extends Node2D

const INK := Color("#3a2a20")

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_circle(Vector2.ZERO, 50.0, Color("#f4d35e"))     # the face
	draw_circle(Vector2(-18, -14), 6.0, INK)              # eyes
	draw_circle(Vector2(18, -14), 6.0, INK)
	draw_arc(Vector2(0, 4), 26.0, 0.5, PI - 0.5, 16, INK, 3.0)    # a smile
	draw_line(Vector2(-44, -44), Vector2(44, -44), INK, 6.0)      # the brim of a hat

tests.label: draw_circle is used at least three times: the face and two eyes
tests.why: An eye is a small circle: draw_circle(Vector2(-18, -14), 6.0, INK)

tests.label: draw_arc is used for the smile
tests.why: draw_arc(centre, radius, start angle, end angle, point count, colour, width)

tests.label: draw_line is used
tests.why: draw_line(from, to, colour, width)

tests.label: _draw() runs without an error

hints: An eye: draw_circle(Vector2(-18, -14), 6.0, INK). Negative y is above the middle of the face.
A smile: draw_arc(Vector2(0, 4), 26.0, 0.5, PI - 0.5, 16, INK, 3.0). Swap the two angles for PI + 0.5 and TAU - 0.5 and it frowns.
A brim: draw_line(Vector2(-44, -44), Vector2(44, -44), INK, 6.0).
explain: Try a nose from three points: draw_colored_polygon([Vector2(0, -6), Vector2(6, 6), Vector2(-6, 6)], INK). And notice that you drew the eyes after the face. Put them first and they vanish – the reason is the third section of this chapter.

title: Fix the bug: the bar that will not fill
task:
This bar should fill over four seconds. Press Play and it sits empty, although charge is counting up exactly as it should. The line of text under it tells you why.

Make the bar fill. One line is enough.
starter:
extends Node2D

var charge := 0.0      # 0 is empty, 1 is full
var draws := 0         # how many times _draw() has run

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	charge = minf(charge + delta * 0.25, 1.0)

func _draw() -> void:
	draws += 1
	draw_rect(Rect2(-80, -8, 160, 16), Color("#2b2440"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(-80, -8, 160.0 * charge, 16), Color("#8fd36a"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(-80, 30), "_draw() has run %d times" % draws, HORIZONTAL_ALIGNMENT_LEFT, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)
solution:
extends Node2D

var charge := 0.0      # 0 is empty, 1 is full
var draws := 0         # how many times _draw() has run

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	charge = minf(charge + delta * 0.25, 1.0)
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draws += 1
	draw_rect(Rect2(-80, -8, 160, 16), Color("#2b2440"))
	draw_rect(Rect2(-80, -8, 160.0 * charge, 16), Color("#8fd36a"))
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(-80, 30), "_draw() has run %d times" % draws, HORIZONTAL_ALIGNMENT_LEFT, -1, 12, Color.WHITE)

tests.label: after two seconds, charge is 0.5
and _draw() has run many times, not once
but never more than once a frame

hints: The value changes in _process. That is where to say the picture is out of date.
Add queue_redraw() as the last line of _process.
explain: Everybody who learns _draw() meets this bug in their first hour: the numbers are right and the screen is stale. When a drawing does not change, the first question is always "did I ask?". This fix asks every frame, even once the bar is full and nothing is changing; the first tutorial below does better.

title: Fix the bug: where has the hill gone?
task:
This should be a sun going down behind a green hill, under a blue sky. Press Play: there is no hill at all, and the sun is whole.

All three helpers are correct. Put the three calls in _draw() into the right order. (drawn records the order for the checks; leave it alone.)
starter:
extends Node2D

var drawn: Array = []     # the order things were painted in

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func _draw() -> void:
	drawn.clear()
	_hill()
	_sky()
	_sun()

func _sky() -> void:
	drawn.append("sky")
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#9fd3e8"))

func _sun() -> void:
	drawn.append("sun")
	draw_circle(Vector2(200, 120), 30.0, Color("#f4d35e"))

func _hill() -> void:
	drawn.append("hill")
	draw_circle(Vector2(160, 330), 220.0, Color("#6aa84f"))
solution:

var drawn: Array = []     # the order things were painted in

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO   # draw from the top-left corner of the view

func _draw() -> void:
	drawn.clear()
	_sky()
	_sun()
	_hill()

func _sky() -> void:
	drawn.append("sky")
	draw_rect(Rect2(0, 0, 320, 180), Color("#9fd3e8"))

func _sun() -> void:
	drawn.append("sun")

func _hill() -> void:
