tests.label: painted back to front: sky, then sun, then hill

hints: The sky is a rectangle the size of the whole view. Whatever is drawn before it is painted over.
Furthest away first: _sky(), _sun(), _hill().
explain: The hill is one enormous circle with its centre far below the view; only its top shows. Now make the sun set: change its y from 120 to 150 and it sinks behind the hill, with no code to work out which part of it is hidden. Order did that.

title: Dots in a row
task: The row of dots under a set of pages: five of them, 20 pixels apart, with the middle one on the origin. Write dot_pos(i) to return the centre of dot i (0 to 4). Then draw all five in _draw() with a loop and draw_circle, radius 4 – the dot numbered current in white, the others in Color(1, 1, 1, 0.35).
starter:
extends Node2D

const COUNT := 5
const GAP := 20.0

var current := 1

func dot_pos(i: int) -> Vector2:
	return Vector2.ZERO

func _draw() -> void:
	pass

tests.label: the middle dot is on the origin
a loop draws each dot at dot_pos(i)
tests.why: for i in COUNT: then draw_circle(dot_pos(i), 4.0, colour)

tests.label: _draw() runs without an error

hints: Dot 2 is at x = 0, and each step of i is 20 pixels: (i - 2) * GAP.
A colour chosen in one line: Color.WHITE if i == current else Color(1, 1, 1, 0.35).
explain: The solution writes the 2 as (COUNT - 1) / 2.0, so that changing COUNT to 7 keeps the row centred. Change current and the bright dot moves – state in a variable, picture from the state.

title: A board of squares
task:
Draw a chessboard: 8 by 8 cells of 16 pixels, centred on the origin, so its top-left corner is at (−64, −64). Write two helpers and use them in a loop inside a loop:

  • cell_rect(col, row) -> Rect2 – the square for a cell; column 0 is on the left and row 0 at the top;
  • is_dark(col, row) -> bool – the top-left cell is light, and the colours alternate along rows and down columns.

Use any two colours you like.

tests.label: cell_rect(3, 5): column 3 across, row 5 down
the top-left cell is light
two loops, one inside the other, draw each cell_rect
tests.why: for row in 8: for col in 8: draw_rect(cell_rect(col, row), …)

tests.label: _draw() runs without an error

hints: The x of a cell is the left edge of the board plus whole cells: -64 + col * CELL. The y is the same with row.
Add the column and the row. Neighbours differ by one, so odd and even alternate: (col + row) % 2 == 1.
explain: Sixty-four calls from three lines. Any grid – a board, an inventory, a tile map, a level editor – is these two helpers and this double loop; only what goes in each cell changes.

title: Predict: how many drawings?
task:
Predict, then check. Read the script without playing it. It runs for 2.75 seconds, which at the frame rate the checks use is 44 frames. How many times has _draw() run by then? Type your answer into guess and press Check.

If you are wrong, add print(draws) to _draw(), press Play and watch.
starter:
extends Node2D

var guess := -1       # your prediction

var t := 0.0
var shown := 0
var draws := 0

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	t += delta
	position.x += 10.0 * delta
	var now := int(t * 2.0)
	if now != shown:
		shown = now
		queue_redraw()
		queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draws += 1
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(-8, 8), str(shown), HORIZONTAL_ALIGNMENT_LEFT, -1, 24, Color.WHITE)
solution:
extends Node2D

var guess := 6        # once at the start, then once for each of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5

var t := 0.0
var shown := 0
var draws := 0

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	t += delta
	position.x += 10.0 * delta
	var now := int(t * 2.0)
	if now != shown:
		shown = now
		queue_redraw()
		queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draws += 1
	draw_string(ThemeDB.fallback_font, Vector2(-8, 8), str(shown), HORIZONTAL_ALIGNMENT_LEFT, -1, 24, Color.WHITE)

tests.label: guess is the number of times _draw() ran in 2.75 seconds

hints: Three things are trying to mislead you: the node moves every frame, queue_redraw() is called twice in a row, and something happens before any of it.
int(t * 2.0) changes every half second. How many times does it change in 2.75 seconds? And how many drawings were there before the first change?
explain: Six. A node is drawn once when it first appears, showing 0. The number then changes at 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 and 2.5 seconds: five more. Moving position every frame costs no drawings, because the kept drawing is moved. And asking twice is asking once.

title: A bar chart
task:
Turn DATA into a chart. Write bar_rect(i), the rectangle for the bar of DATA[i]:

  • every bar is BAR_W wide, with GAP between neighbours, and the whole row is centred on x = 0;
  • every bar stands on the line y = BASE_Y and rises from it;
  • the bar of the largest value is MAX_H tall and the others are in proportion.

Then draw the bars with a loop, and the line they stand on with draw_line.

tests.label: the tallest bar, of 12, is 80 tall and stands on y = 40
the first bar, of 3, starts at x = −66 and is 20 tall
the last bar, of 9, ends at x = 66 and is 60 tall
the bar of 7 is 46.67 tall
and its bottom is on the line
a loop draws each bar_rect
tests.why: for i in DATA.size(): then draw_rect(bar_rect(i), colour)

tests.label: draw_line draws the line they stand on
tests.why: draw_line(Vector2(-76, BASE_Y), Vector2(76, BASE_Y), Color.WHITE, 2.0)

tests.label: _draw() runs without an error

hints: Five bars and four gaps are 5 * 20 + 4 * 8 = 132 pixels, so the first bar starts at x = −66 and each one after it is BAR_W + GAP further right.
The height is the share of the largest value: MAX_H * DATA[i] / DATA.max().
y grows downwards, so the top of a bar is BASE_Y - h and the rectangle is Rect2(x, BASE_Y - h, BAR_W, h).
explain: Change a number in DATA, or add a sixth, and the chart rearranges itself: nothing in it was placed by hand. For a finishing touch, write each value above its bar with draw_string at bar_rect(i).position + Vector2(4, -4).

title: A circle out of squares
task:
This is the game's draw_pixel_disc, with its heart taken out. _draw() paints a disc as rows of big square "pixels", UNIT across: for each row it asks half_width(dy) how many pixels wide the disc is on each side of the middle. At the moment the answer is always R, so it draws a square.

Write half_width. Row dy runs from -R to R - 1 and covers the strip from y = dy to y = dy + 1, so its middle is at y = dy + 0.5. A circle of radius R at height y reaches sqrt(R * R - y * y) out from its centre. Return that, rounded to the nearest whole number of pixels, as an int.

tests.label: the rows beside the middle are the full 6 wide (an int)
the top row is 2 wide on each side
and so is the bottom row
_draw() runs without an error

hints: Start with the middle of the row: var y := dy + 0.5.
Rounding a positive float to the nearest whole number: add 0.5 and cut off the fraction with int().
return int(sqrt(R * R - y * y) + 0.5)
explain: Twelve rectangles, and a circle that belongs in a pixel-art game. Measuring each row at its middle, the + 0.5 on dy, is what makes the top half and the bottom half mirror each other. Change UNIT to 2.0 and R to 18: the same disc, in finer pixels. The game's version is this with a colour, a centre and a guard against a negative square root.

title: The scale for a pack
task: Your game draws everything at DENSITY screen pixels per art pixel. Finish scale_for(per), where per is how many file pixels a pack uses for one art pixel. It returns the whole-number scale that pack needs, or 0 if no whole number will do.
starter:
extends Node

const DENSITY := 6

func scale_for(per: int) -> int:
	return 0

tests.label: a pack saved one to one needs scale 6
a pack saved three to one needs scale 2
four to one cannot reach 6: scale_for(4) is 0

hints: The scale is DENSITY / per, but only when that division has nothing left over.
DENSITY % per is the remainder. If it is not zero, return 0 before dividing.
explain: Without the remainder test, scale_for(4) would quietly return 1 and that pack would be drawn at four screen pixels per art pixel beside everything else's six. A function that refuses is more use than one that guesses.

title: Predict, then check: the ragged row
task: widths(count, scale) is the function from this chapter: how many screen pixels each texel gets. Do not run it yet. Work out by hand what it returns for four texels at a scale of 2.5 and at 1.5, and write your answers into guess_a and guess_b. Then press Check.

tests.label: guess_a is what widths(4, 2.5) returns
guess_b is what widths(4, 1.5) returns

hints: At 2.5 there are ten screen pixels, numbered 0 to 9. For each, work out int((x + 0.5) / 2.5): pixel 0 gives 0, pixel 1 gives 0, pixel 2 gives 1…
Four texels cannot share ten pixels evenly, so the answer is twos and threes. The first texel gets the smaller share.
explain: At 1.5 it is worse than uneven: half the texels are twice as wide as the others. This is what the two "uneven" sprites in the demo at the top of the chapter are doing. Add print(widths(4, 2.5)) in a _ready() to see it for yourself.

title: How wide are the bars?
task: Write bars(base, window). The game is base in size and is drawn in window at the largest whole scale that fits – but never less than 1, as Godot's integer scale mode does. Return a Vector2i: the width of the bar at each side, and the height of the bar above and below. If the window is too small, the numbers come out negative: that much of the game is cut off.

tests.label: 320 x 180 in 1920 x 1080: no bars
in 1366 x 768: 43 at the sides, 24 above and below
in 300 x 200 the scale stays 1: ten pixels cut off each side

hints: First the scale: the smaller of window.x / base.x and window.y / base.y, and then maxi(1, …) so it is never zero.
What is drawn is base * n. What is spare is window - base * n, and half of that goes on each side.
explain: Vector2i does whole-number arithmetic on both parts at once, so the three lines of the letterbox example collapse into one. A spare 87 pixels gives a bar of 43 on each side and one pixel that belongs to neither, which the engine puts on one of them.

title: Fix the bug: the walker who never arrives
task: This walker should cover 20 pixels a second and always be drawn on a whole pixel. Somebody put the rounding in the wrong place. At 60 frames a second she does not move at all; at 30 she goes half as fast again as she should. Change step() and drawn() so that pos stays exact and only the drawing is rounded. Leave where_after() as it is: the checks use it.

tests.label: one second at 60 frames a second: drawn at (30, 40)
one second at 30 frames a second: the same place
ten frames at 60: drawn at (13, 40)
and pos.x is still the exact 13.33

hints: At 60 frames a second one step is a third of a pixel. What is round(10.33)? And the frame after?
Take .round() out of step() and put it in drawn().
explain: Rounding the stored position throws away the part of each step that is smaller than half a pixel, and at a high frame rate that is all of it. At 30 frames a second each step is two thirds of a pixel, which rounds up to a whole one, so she covers 30 pixels where she should cover 20. A bug that depends on the frame rate is the hardest kind to notice on your own machine. Keep the truth exact and round on the way to the screen.

title: Fit the phone
task:
Do what Little Hours does on a phone. fit(screen) returns a Dictionary with two keys. "scale" is the largest whole number of screen pixels per game pixel at which a view of at least MIN_VIEW still fits both ways, and never less than 1. "view" is a Vector2i: the screen divided by that scale, in whole numbers.

Then write lost(screen): the Vector2i of screen pixels left over, because the view times the scale can fall a pixel or two short of the screen.

tests.label: and a view of 960 x 540
2856 x 1280: three would fit across but only two down, so scale 2
and a view of 1428 x 640
a screen smaller than MIN_VIEW still gets scale 1
nothing lost on 1920 x 1080
one pixel each way lost on 2401 x 1081

hints: The scale is the same sum as whole_scale, with MIN_VIEW as the view, and maxi(1, …) round it.
The view is Vector2i(screen.x / n, screen.y / n) – integer division again, on purpose.
For lost: call fit, take the two values out of the Dictionary, and return screen - view * n.
explain: With a fixed view, the screen has to be an exact multiple of the game or there are bars. Turn the sum round and the loss is never more than n - 1 pixels each way: a sliver instead of a letterbox. What you give up is a fixed view. The interface and the camera have to cope with 960 × 540 on one phone and 1428 × 640 on another.

title: Amount to decibels, and back
task: Write to_db(amount: float) -> float (20 × log10 of the amount) and from_db(db: float) -> float (10 to the power of db / 20). There is no log10 here: log() is the natural logarithm, so divide by log(10.0).

tests.label: to_db(1.0) is 0: unchanged
half is about -6 dB
a tenth is -20 dB
double is +6 dB
-20 dB is a tenth
one undoes the other

hints: Written with log: 20.0 * log(amount) / log(10.0).
The reverse is pow(10.0, db / 20.0).
explain: In Godot itself these are linear_to_db and db_to_linear. Written out they show what is going on: a multiplication of volumes is an addition of decibels, which is why a log is there.

title: Fix the bug: a slider that is silent too soon
task: level_to_db(level) turns a slider from 0 to 1 into a volume in decibels. It is "right" at both ends, 0 dB at full and -80 at nothing, but at half-way the game is almost inaudible. Fix it so that 0.5 gives about -6 dB, and so that a slider at 0 still gives exactly -80 and does not crash.

tests.label: full is 0 dB
half the slider is about -6 dB
a tenth is -20 dB
nothing is -80 dB
so is something too small to hear

hints: A straight line in dB is the wrong shape. Half the volume is about 6 dB less, not 40.
Return early for a level that is near 0, so that you never take the log of 0; otherwise 20.0 * log(level) / log(10.0).
explain: The straight line crams the whole usable range into the top of the slider. The log mapping spreads it evenly, and the early return is the guard clause from Chapter F: deal with the case with no answer first.

title: Predict, then check
task:
Work these out by hand, then put your answers into the guess variables and check.

  • guess_a: the decibels of an amount of 0.1, as a whole number
  • guess_b: the decibels of an amount of 2.0, rounded to a whole number
  • guess_c: the frequency of MIDI note 81, the A an octave above 440, as a whole number
  • guess_d: how many samples are in half a second at a rate of 22050

tests.label: guess_a is the decibels of 0.1
guess_b is the decibels of 2.0
guess_c is the frequency of MIDI note 81
guess_d is the samples in half a second

hints: A tenth is -20 dB and a doubling is +6. Twelve semitones is an octave, which doubles the frequency.
Samples are the rate times the seconds: 22050 × 0.5.
explain: -20, 6, 880 and 11025. The first two are the "numbers worth remembering" from the decibels section. The third is the octave: note 81 is 12 semitones above 69, and an octave is exactly a doubling. The last is a reminder of why game sounds are kept short: even half a second is eleven thousand numbers.

title: The frequency of a note
task: Write note_freq(midi: int) -> float: 440.0 times two to the power of the number of semitones from note 69, divided by 12. Notes below 69 must come out lower than 440, which is where a whole-number division would let you down.

tests.label: note 69 is 440 Hz
an octave up is double
an octave down is half
middle C is about 261.63
one semitone above A is about 466.16

hints: The exponent is (midi - 69) / 12, and it must keep its fraction. Make at least one side a float.
return 440.0 * pow(2.0, float(midi - 69) / 12.0)
explain: With (midi - 69) / 12 in whole numbers, middle C would be an exponent of -9 / 12 = 0, so 440 Hz: a note that is not C at all. A semitone is a ratio, not a step, and the ratio only exists as a fraction.

title: One cycle of a square wave
task: Write square_cycle(n: int) -> Array, which returns n samples (an even number) of one cycle of a square wave: the first half 1.0, the second half -1.0. So square_cycle(4) is [1.0, 1.0, -1.0, -1.0].

tests.label: square_cycle(4)  →  [1, 1, -1, -1]
no samples: an empty array

hints: Build an array in a loop with append. Whether sample i is in the first half is i < n / 2.
out.append(1.0 if i < n / 2 else -1.0)
explain: This is square() from the chapter, evaluated at n evenly spaced points instead of one. Every waveform the game makes is a loop like this one, with a different line inside it. (Here the integer division is exactly what you want, since n is even.)

title: Fade out the last samples
task: Write fade_out(samples: Array, fade: int) -> Array. It returns a new array of the same length in which each of the final fade samples is multiplied by (n - i) / fade, with n the number of samples and i the sample's index, so the ramp comes down to 1 / fade at the end. The others are unchanged. The array you were given must not be changed. For eight ones and a fade of 4, you get [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25].

tests.label: eight ones, fade 4
four ones, fade 2
a fade of 0 changes nothing
an empty sound stays empty
a fade as long as the sound starts at full and ends at 1/5
the length is unchanged

hints: Make a new array, loop over the indexes, and for the ones in the last fade multiply by the ramp. Index i is in the fade when i >= n - fade.
Inside the if: v *= float(n - i) / float(fade). With a fade of 0 the if is never true, so you never divide by it.
explain: This is the cure for the click at the end of a sound, done by hand. The envelope from the chapter does it with a formula; this does it on a list that already exists. Notice that the float()s are needed: (n - i) / fade in whole numbers would be 0 for every sample but the first.

title: One anchored edge
task: Write edge(parent_len: float, anchor: float, offset: float) -> float: how far along the parent the edge is. edge(320.0, 1.0, -10.0) is 310.

tests.label: right-anchored, 10 in: 310
left-anchored, 10 in: 10
centre-anchored, 20 left of the middle: 220
right-anchored in a wider parent: 950

hints: The anchor says how far across the parent; the offset is pixels from there.
return parent_len * anchor + offset
explain: One line, and every anchored control on every screen is made of four of them. The anchor scales with the parent and the offset does not, which is why a control with both anchors at 1 sticks to the right edge.

title: Fix the bug: a column that is too tall

tests.label: three controls, two gaps: 140
one control has no gap at all
four controls, three gaps: 58

hints: How many gaps are there between three controls? Between one?
One fewer gap than there are controls: gap * (heights.size() - 1).
explain: The fence-post error: three posts, two spaces. It is the same line as needed in the tutorial, and an extra gap at the end is a real bug in a real layout, a strip of nothing at the bottom of every card. (With an empty list this gives a negative gap, and a real container guards for that; for this exercise lists are never empty.)

title: Predict, then check
task:
These functions are written for you. Work out the answers by hand and put them in the guess variables. Then check.

  • guess_a: edge(400.0, 1.0, -16.0)
  • guess_b: edge(400.0, 0.5, -50.0)
  • guess_c: how much leftover room a row 300 wide has with three children of minimum 40, 60 and 80 and gaps of 10, as leftover(300.0, [40.0, 60.0, 80.0], 10.0)

tests.label: guess_a is edge(400, 1, -16)
guess_b is edge(400, 0.5, -50)
guess_c is the leftover in a 300 wide row
guess_d is the leftover in a 150 wide row

hints: The first two are an anchor times a length, plus an offset. In the row, the minimums add to 180 and the two gaps to 20.

title: Share by stretch ratio
task: Containers can give one child more of the spare room than another with a stretch ratio. Write share(leftover: float, ratios: Array) -> Array: it splits leftover among the children in proportion to their ratios. A ratio of 0 means "does not expand" and gets 0. If every ratio is 0, everyone gets 0. For 120 and ratios [1, 0, 2] the answer is [40, 0, 80].

tests.label: equal ratios share equally
nobody expands: nobody gets any
one child takes it all
nothing to share

hints: Add up the ratios first. Each child gets leftover * ratio / total – unless the total is 0.
A one-line if that guards the division: leftover * r / total if total > 0.0 else 0.0.
explain: This is size_flags_stretch_ratio: two expanding children with ratios 1 and 2 get a third and two thirds of what is left. The tutorial used equal shares, which is a ratio of 1 for each. The guard is the thing everyone forgets: with nobody expanding, the total is 0 and the division would be by zero.

title: Is it big enough for a thumb?
task: Write thumb_ok(size: Vector2, view: Vector2) -> bool: a control is big enough when both its width and its height are at least a tenth of the view's height. In a view 540 tall, 54 is the smallest side that passes.
solution:
extends Node

func thumb_ok(size: Vector2, view: Vector2) -> bool:
	var least := view.y * 0.1
	return size.x >= least and size.y >= least

tests.label: a 200 by 64 button in a 960 by 540 view
48 is under 54: too short
40 is under 54: too narrow
exactly a tenth passes
the rule follows the view: 36 is enough in 360

hints: The smallest allowed side is view.y * 0.1, for both sides.
return size.x >= least and size.y >= least
explain: Both sides, because a button that is tall and thin is as hard to hit as a short one. >= because exactly a tenth passes. The game's own test only checks the button's height, since its buttons stretch to the container's width, but a control placed by hand should pass for both.

title: How many columns fit?
task: A GridContainer needs a number of columns. Write columns_that_fit(width: int, cell: int, gap: int) -> int: the largest n for which n cells and the n - 1 gaps between them fit in width, and never fewer than 1. For a width of 320, cells of 64 and gaps of 8, the answer is 4 (4 × 64 + 3 × 8 = 280; 5 × 64 + 4 × 8 = 352 is too wide).

tests.label: 320 wide, 64 cells, 8 gaps: 4 columns
352 is exactly enough for 5
and 351 is one short
never fewer than one column
with no gaps: 10 cells of 64

hints: Pretend there is one extra gap at the end, so that every cell has one after it: then n cells take n * (cell + gap), and the room is width + gap.
maxi(1, (width + gap) / (cell + gap)). The whole-number division is the point here: you want the whole number of cells that fit.
explain: The trick is to add one gap to the width, so every cell comes with its gap and the sum is a plain division. Integer division, which was a trap in Chapter D, is what you are after: it throws the part of a cell that does not fit away. maxi(1, ...) is the guard so that a very narrow screen still gets one column.

title: There and back
task: Write both directions for a very small save. save_text(coins, day) returns JSON text for a Dictionary with the keys "coins" and "day". coins_in(text) takes text like that and returns the coins as an int. You may assume the text is a good save.

and day 3
coins_in() reads 30, as an int
what one writes, the other reads

hints: JSON.stringify() wants one value. Build the Dictionary inside the call: {"coins": coins, "day": day}.
For the way back: JSON.parse_string(text) gives a Dictionary, and the number in it is a float until you put it through int().

title: Predict: what survives the trip?
task: Predict, then check. Three values go through JSON.stringify and back through JSON.parse_string. Before running anything, change each "?" to what you think the value comes back as. Then press Run, which prints the truth, and see how you did.

func kind(v: Variant) -> String:

extends Node

var key_is := "String"    # the key in {7: "seven"}:  "int" or "String"
var spot_is := "String"   # a Vector2(3, 4):          "Vector2", "Array" or "String"

func kind(v: Variant) -> String:
	match typeof(v):
		TYPE_INT: return "int"
		TYPE_FLOAT: return "float"
		TYPE_STRING: return "String"

		TYPE_VECTOR2: return "Vector2"

func trip(v: Variant) -> Variant:

func _ready() -> void:
	print("the day comes back as a ", kind(trip({"day": 3})["day"]))

	print("the spot comes back as a ", kind(trip({"spot": Vector2(3, 4)})["spot"]))

tests.label: your prediction for the day is right
your prediction for the key is right
your prediction for the spot is right

hints: JSON has one kind of number, and its keys are always text.
JSON has no idea what a Vector2 is. Godot writes the nearest thing it can, in quotes.
explain: All three change. Numbers come back as float, keys come back as String, and a Vector2 comes back as a String that reads (3.0, 4.0) and is no more a vector than this sentence is. A loader converts the first with int(); the other two are avoided by saving String keys and plain numbers in the first place.

title: Fix the bug: the loader that falls over
task: This loader works on the save its author tested it with and stops the game on nearly anything else. Fix load_coins(text) so that it always returns a sensible int: the saved coins when they are a number, never less than 0; and 0 when the text is not JSON, is not a Dictionary, has no "coins", or has coins that are not a number.

tests.label: a good save still loads: 42
text that is not JSON gives 0
a list gives 0
a save with no coins gives 0
coins that are text give 0
negative coins give 0

hints: There are two places it can stop: data may not be a Dictionary at all, and if it is, it may have no "coins". Deal with them in that order.
data.get("coins") gives null for a missing key, where data["coins"] stops the game. Test its type before you use it.
Last line: return maxi(0, int(data["coins"])).

title: Only what the shop sells
task: A bag is saved as a Dictionary of item names and counts, like {"carrot": 3, "tomato": 1}. Write clean_bag(v), which takes whatever the file had under "bag" and returns a bag the game can trust: only items in KNOWN, only counts that are numbers, each made a whole number, and nothing with a count below 1. If v is not a Dictionary at all, return an empty one.

tests.label: a good bag comes through
with whole-number counts
an item the game does not have is dropped
a count that is not a number is dropped
counts below 1 are dropped
something that is not a Dictionary gives an empty bag
and so does nothing at all

hints: Start with an empty Dictionary and add to it. Never take things out of the one you were given.
for key in v: walks the names. Two tests decide whether one is worth keeping: KNOWN.has(key), and the usual number test on v[key].
Convert first, then judge: var n := int(v[key]), and add it only if n > 0.
explain: This is the sanitiser's idea one level down: a nested value gets a small function of its own that builds a clean copy. Little Hours has two like it – _known_counts() for the crops and fish you are carrying, _free_counts() for the scores – and its _sanitize() calls them the way yours would call this.

title: A code you could post to yourself
task:
A backup code is a save as one line of text a player can copy somewhere safe. Write the pair.

make_code(data) returns LH-1:, then the number of characters in the JSON, then :, then the JSON – so make_code({"coins": 5}) is LH-1:11:{"coins":5}.

read_code(text) returns the Dictionary inside a code, or an empty Dictionary if anything is wrong with it: it does not start with LH-1:, the JSON is not the length the code says (it was cut short in the post), or what is inside is not a Dictionary. Spaces and line ends around the code are ignored.

tests.label: make_code({"coins": 5}) is LH-1:11:{"coins":5}
read_code() gets the 5 coins back out
what one makes, the other reads
spaces and a line end around the code are ignored
a code cut short gives {}
a code with the wrong start gives {}
a code with a list inside gives {}
something that is not a code gives {}

hints: For make_code, keep the JSON in a variable so you can ask its .length(), then build the line with "%s:%d:%s" % [HEADER, json.length(), json].
To take a code apart, do not split on : – the JSON is full of colons. Check begins_with(HEADER + ":"), cut that off with .substr(), then .find(":") gives the position of the colon after the number.

Everything before that colon is the length (int(rest.substr(0, colon))); everything after is the JSON (rest.substr(colon + 1)). Compare the JSON's real length with the promised one before you parse it.
explain: The length is the cheapest check there is and it catches the commonest damage: most of a code is still valid-looking text. Little Hours's backup_code() has this shape – header, length, payload – with the payload compressed first, and it goes one step further than read_code: a separate function says what is wrong, in words a player can act on, so the card can answer a bad paste with "the code is cut short" instead of a shrug.

title: How long to go?
task: A watering can was used at used_at seconds on the game's clock, and takes cooldown seconds to refill. Write cooldown_left(used_at, now, cooldown): how many seconds are still to go at time now. It is never less than 0.

tests.label: used at 10, now 10.5, cooldown 2: 1.5 to go
used this instant: the whole cooldown to go
exactly ready: 0
long ready: still 0, not a negative number

hints: It is ready at used_at + cooldown. How far away is that from now?
Wrap the subtraction in maxf(0.0, …) so that a can which has been ready for ages does not report -18 seconds.

title: Fix the bug: the stopwatch that ran fast
task: This stopwatch times a race. Its author tested it on a 60 Hz monitor, where it was perfect, and then the complaints came in from people with other screens. Fix it so that seconds() is right whatever the frame rate. play() is there to play frames for the tests; leave it as it is.

tests.label: 60 frames at 60 a second: 1 second
then 120 frames at 120 a second: 2 seconds in all
then 15 frames at 30 a second: 2.5 seconds in all

hints: The 60 in seconds() is the bug: it is the author's monitor, written into the game.
Each call to _process is told how long its frame was. Keep a float and add that to it.
explain: The first check passes before you change anything, which is the whole trouble with this bug: on the machine it was written on, it is not there.

title: Predict: who speaks first?
task: Predict, then check. Five things are said by the code below. Before running it, put the five in prediction in the order you think they are said, first to last. Then press Run to see the order for real.

var prediction: Array = []     # e.g. ["toast", "egg", …] – all five, in order

func say(word: String) -> void:

	print(word)

func _ready() -> void:

tests.label: prediction has five things in it
and they are in the order they were said

hints: A call to later() returns as soon as it reaches its await. So what is the first thing that actually gets said?
Work out the time on the clock for each: the egg at 0.5, tea at 1.0 – and the washing up is started at 1.0, so it is said at 1.25.

title: Paid every two seconds, hitch or no hitch
task: A market stall earns one coin every GAP seconds. Write tick(delta), called once a frame: add the time to wait, and add a coin for every full gap that has gone by. A long frame must not lose money – if delta covers three gaps, that is three coins – and whatever is left over after the last coin stays in wait.
starter:
extends Node

const GAP := 2.0

var wait := 0.0
var coins := 0

func tick(delta: float) -> void:
	pass
solution:
extends Node

const GAP := 2.0

var wait := 0.0
var coins := 0

func tick(delta: float) -> void:
	wait += delta
	while wait >= GAP:
		wait -= GAP
		coins += 1

tests.label: after 1 second: nothing yet
after 2 seconds: 1 coin
after 3.5 seconds: still 1
then one frame of 5 seconds: 4 coins, all three gaps paid
with the half second left over still in wait
so 1.5 seconds more makes 5

hints: Start from the gull example: add delta, then if wait >= GAP: take a gap off and pay.
An if pays once. What pays again and again for as long as there is a whole gap left?
while wait >= GAP: with wait -= GAP and coins += 1 inside.
explain: The only difference from the gull is one word, while for if, and it decides what a hitch costs the player. With if, a five-second freeze pays one coin and the other two arrive on the next two frames, which nobody would notice; with wait = 0.0 as well, they would be gone.

title: A clock that comes round
task: A day and night last DAY_LENGTH real seconds, starting at midnight. t is the number of seconds since the game began – possibly many days' worth. Write hour_text(t), the time of day as 24-hour "HH:MM", and is_night(t), which is true before 06:00 and from 21:00 on.

tests.label: the game starts at 00:00
a quarter of the day in, 06:00
15 seconds in, 01:30
195 seconds in, 19:30
a whole day in, 00:00 again – not 24:00
ten days and 210 seconds in, 21:00
04:30 is night
06:00 is day
19:30 is day
21:00 is night
03:00 on the second day is night

hints: First get rid of the whole days: fmod(t, DAY_LENGTH) is the seconds into today.
A day has 1440 minutes. Seconds into today, divided by DAY_LENGTH, times 1440, made an int, is minutes since midnight. A helper function for that serves both answers.
Hours are m / 60 and minutes m % 60, both with %02d. Night is m < 360 or m >= 1260.
explain: Both answers are worked out from t and neither is stored, so they cannot fall out of step. Dividing two ints throws the remainder away (Chapter D), which is a trap almost everywhere and exactly right for the hour.

title: The kettle that is already on
task: Write boil(). It prints click, waits three seconds, and prints whistle. But if it is called while the kettle is still on, it prints already on and does nothing else – no second click, no second whistle. Use boiling to remember. _ready() is written for you and should print exactly: click, already on, whistle, click, whistle.
starter:
extends Node

var boiling := false

func boil() -> void:
	print("click")
	print("whistle")

func _ready() -> void:
	boil()
	boil()              # too soon: the first is still going
	await get_tree().create_timer(5.0).timeout
	boil()              # long after: fine
solution:
extends Node

var boiling := false

func boil() -> void:
	if boiling:
		print("already on")
		return
	boiling = true
	print("click")
	await get_tree().create_timer(3.0).timeout
	print("whistle")
	boiling = false

func _ready() -> void:
	boil()
	boil()              # too soon: the first is still going
	await get_tree().create_timer(5.0).timeout
	boil()              # long after: fine

tests.label: prints click, already on, whistle, click, whistle
when everything has finished, boiling is false again
waits with await get_tree().create_timer(…).timeout
tests.why: The three seconds should be a real wait.

hints: Put the wait in first: await get_tree().create_timer(3.0).timeout between the two prints. Run it and see what the second call does.
Now the guard, at the very top: if boiling: print and return.
Set boiling = true before the wait and false after the whistle. If you forget the second, the third call will be turned away too.
explain: A coroutine that can be started while it is still running needs to know that it is. The flag goes up before the await and comes down after it, and the check sits above both. This is also why the phone in Little Hours has a _buzzing flag: its shake is a loop of short awaited timers, and a second text arriving mid-shake must not start a second one.

title: A static helper
task: Write static func coins_text(n: int) -> String that returns "1 coin" for exactly one and "N coins" otherwise – including "0 coins" and negative numbers like "-3 coins". A pure function like this is what belongs in a class_name script rather than in an autoload.

tests.label: one coin, singular
zero is plural
negative numbers keep their sign

title: Fix the bug: the back door

title: Look it up, or fall back
task: grow_time(id) stops the script when it is asked about a crop that is not in the table, or one whose entry has no "grow". Make it return the crop's grow time when there is one, and 20.0 in both of the other cases.

tests.label: grow_time("tomato")  →  20.0 (in the table, but no grow)
grow_time("turnip")  →  20.0 (not in the table)

title: Whose price is it?
task: Predict, then check. This shop prints the price of a pumpkin and then the price of a carrot. A pumpkin is 15 and a carrot has no price of its own, so it should print 15 and then 5. Run it, see what it prints, and fix of() so that the output is right – without changing either table.

tests.label: prints 15, then 5
defaults is as it was written
a carrot is still a carrot

hints: var crop: Dictionary = defaults does not make a new dictionary. It gives the one dictionary a second name (Chapter G).
Every value the loop writes goes into defaults itself, and stays there for the next call. Start from defaults.duplicate().
explain: It printed 15 twice: the pumpkin's price was written into the shared defaults and the carrot inherited it. This is the resource-sharing trap in miniature – one object, two names, and a change through one seen through the other. The table of defaults should be something nobody ever writes to.

title: What is missing?
task: Write missing(table, required). table is a dictionary of entries like the ones in this chapter and required is an array of keys every entry must have. Return an array with one string for each key that an entry lacks, as "id: key", in the table's order and then the order of required. A table with nothing missing gives [].

tests.label: nothing required, nothing missing
an empty entry lacks every required key, in order
a complete table gives []

hints: Two loops, one inside the other: every entry, and for each entry every required key.
if not table[id].has(key): then found.append("%s: %s" % [id, key]).
explain: Because the table and the list of keys are both arguments, this one function checks every table in a game. Little Hours' tests do the same job for its people: each must live in a room that exists and have something to say.

title: Read the file, trust nothing
task:
Write parse_prices(text), which turns the text of a JSON file into a price table.

  • If the text is not JSON, or is not a JSON object, return {"problem": "not an object"}.
  • If the object has no "prices" that is itself an object, return {"problem": "no prices"}.
  • Otherwise return a dictionary of every entry of "prices" whose value is a number, as an int. Entries that are not numbers are left out.

So {"prices": {"carrot": 4, "lamp": "lots"}} gives {"carrot": 4}.

tests.label: a good file gives its prices
the prices are ints, not the floats JSON hands back
a price that is not a number is left out
text that is not JSON is a problem
a JSON list is a problem
an object without prices is a problem
prices that are a list are a problem

hints: JSON.parse_string() gives null for text that is not JSON. if not raw is Dictionary: catches that and a list in one test.
Every number from JSON is a float, so the test for "is a number" is value is float, and the value to store is int(value).
Build a new dictionary and put only good entries in it. Do not return raw["prices"] itself: that is the file's data, unchecked.
explain: The starter works on a good file, which is what makes this kind of bug dangerous: it only shows when the file is wrong, on somebody else's machine. The solution has the shape of the game's parse_town(): refuse what cannot be used, with a reason, and copy what can into a table of your own making.

title: Like a carrot, but purple
task:
Give the table inheritance. An entry may have a "like" key naming another crop; it then starts from that crop in full instead of from DEFAULT, and its own values go on top. Chains can be any length. Change of(id) so that:

  • of("purple_carrot") has the carrot's grow time, its own name and its own price;
  • of("giant_purple_carrot") starts from the purple carrot;
  • the result never contains a "like" key;
  • an unknown id still gives a copy of DEFAULT.

tests.label: a purple carrot is a carrot with its own name and price
the giant one takes the purple carrot's price
and its own grow time
the result has no "like" key
crops without "like" work as before
a carrot is not renamed by its descendants
an unknown id gives the defaults

hints: The only thing that changes is what the crop starts from: DEFAULT.duplicate(), or – when the entry has a "like" – the full crop it names.
"The full crop it names" is of(own["like"]). A function may call itself; each call deals with one link of the chain and the chain ends at an entry with no "like".
Skip the "like" key when copying the entry's own values: if key != "like":.
explain: of() returns a fresh dictionary every time, so the recursive call hands back something safe to write on. A real version would also guard against a chain that loops back on itself (a like b, b like a), which is one more thing for a table check to look for.

title: Nobody of that name
task: This script has a bug: find it from the error and fix it. It should print the room each person is in, and somebody who is not in the list is nowhere. Fixed, it prints harbour and then nowhere. Change room_of(), not the list.

tests.label: room_of("")  →  "nowhere"

hints: The error names a line in room_of() and says the base is Nil: person is null on that line. The first print worked, so it is null only for some ids.
find_person() has a return inside its loop and none after it. When nobody matches, it falls off the end and returns null.
Before using person, test it: if person == null: and return "nowhere".
explain: The line the error named was not wrong in itself; it was the first line to use the null. The null was made in find_person(), by a path with no return. A function that looks something up can always come back empty-handed, and its caller has to decide what that means.

title: One too many
task:
This script has a bug: find it from the error and fix it. It should print the bag as a numbered list starting at 1, and then the last item:

1. carrot
2. tomato
3. pumpkin
Last: pumpkin

Fix one error, run it again, and read what it says now.
hints: The message gives the index that was asked for and the type it was asked of. An array of three things has the indices 0, 1 and 2.
The loop counts 1, 2, 3 because people count from 1. The array counts from 0. The number shown and the index used should differ by one: bag[i - 1].
There is a second error of the same family behind the first. The last index of an array is its size minus one.
explain: Two bugs, and the first error hid the second: a script stops at its first error, so fixing one and running again is the normal rhythm, not a sign that you made things worse. Both were the same confusion between a count, which starts at 1, and an index, which starts at 0.

title: Twelve coins, or 12.0, or neither
task: Predict, then check. Before you run this, decide what it does: does it print You have 12 coins, print You have 12.0 coins, or stop with an error? Then run it, and fix it so that it prints You have 12 coins. load_coins() must keep returning an int.

tests.label: load_coins() returns an int

hints: The message names two types and an operator. Which + on that line has text on one side and a number on the other?
Text joins only to text. Wrap the number in str(), or build the sentence with a format string: "You have %d coins" % load_coins(text).
explain: An error: + will not join a String to an int. The tempting wrong fix is str(saved["coins"]) inside load_coins(), which gives 12.0, because every number in JSON comes back as a float. Writing int(…) where the value comes in makes it a whole number from then on, and the function's return type says so to everyone who calls it.

title: A table of cases
task: When one function needs twenty checks, the checks become a table. Write failing(f: Callable, cases: Array) -> Array. Each case is a two-item array, [input, want]. Call f with each input and return an array of the inputs whose result was not what was wanted, in order. No failures gives [].

tests.label: three right answers: nothing fails
one wrong expectation: its input comes back
it works for any function, and keeps the order
no cases, no failures

hints: A Callable is called with f.call(argument) (Chapter F). Inside the loop, the input is case[0] and the wanted result is case[1].
Start with var bad: Array = []; in the loop, if f.call(case[0]) != case[1]: then bad.append(case[0]); return bad.
explain: This is table-driven testing, and it is Chapter V's idea turned on tests: the cases are data, and one loop is the code. Adding a case is adding a line. The example in _ready() also shows that a test can be the thing that is wrong – the clock stops at 22:00, not 24:00 – which is worth remembering before "fixing" code to satisfy a check.

title: The mistake is upstream
task: This script has a bug: find it from the error and fix it. A basket is read from text such as "carrot:3,tomato:2", and total() adds up how many things are in it; fixed, the script prints Items: 5. The error will name a line. Before you touch that line, ask whether it is wrong, or whether it was handed something wrong. The basket must hold numbers: basket["carrot"] is the int 3.

tests.label: basket["carrot"] is the int 3, not the text "3"
the basket is {"carrot": 3, "tomato": 2}

hints: The error is in total() and names two types, int and String. sum is the int. So basket[item] is a String. Who put a String in the basket?
split() cuts text into pieces of text. "3" is not 3 until something converts it.
In load_basket(): basket[pair[0]] = int(pair[1]). Leave total() alone.
explain: The stack for this error would be total, called by _ready – and the function with the mistake in it is not on the stack at all, because it had finished and returned before the error happened. Bad data made in one place and tripped over in another is the hardest common kind of bug. Writing int() inside total() would have made the error go away and left every other reader of the basket to meet the same text later. Fix data where it comes in.

title: The crop that waited all day
task:
A player writes: "I planted in the evening and went to bed. Next morning the crop just sat there, all day." No error is printed anywhere. Reproduce it with a test, then fix it.

First write scenario(plant_at, sleeps, look_at), a test in three parts. Arrange: set the clock to plant_at and call plant(). Act: if sleeps is true call sleep(); then set the clock to look_at and call tick(). Check: return whether the plot is ready.

Then fix tick(). The clock starts again from 0 every morning, so a planting time later than the clock can only be from before today: treat such a crop as planted at the start of today. A crop planted at 450 the evening before must be ready 20 seconds into the new day, and not yet ready at 10.

tests.label: planted at 100, looked at 115 the same day: ready
planted at 100, looked at 110 the same day: not yet
planted at 450, slept, looked at 20 the next day: ready
planted at 450, slept, looked at 10 the next day: not yet
planted at 0, looked at 14: not yet
_ready() prints true for both scenarios

hints: Write scenario() first, exactly as the task lists it, and run. The first line should say true and the second false: you have reproduced the bug, and now have a test that will tell you when it is gone.
Put a labelled print in tick(): print("now=", clock_t, " planted_at=", plot["planted_at"]). In the evening scenario, what is "now minus then"?
At the top of tick(): if plot["planted_at"] > clock_t: then plot["planted_at"] = 0.0. The rest of the function stays as it is.
explain: This is the bug from Little Hours' _tick_farm(), and the two lines you added are the two lines that fixed it there. Nothing crashed: every line did what it said, and the mistake was an assumption that "now" is always later than "then". Only a test that arranges the awkward case – evening, then morning – can catch that kind, and once written it guards the fix for good.

title: A label for the build
task: Testers should be able to read the build off the title screen. Finish build_label(version, code, debug) so it returns the version name, a space, and the code in brackets – build_label("2.9.0", 39) gives 2.9.0 (39) – with debug added on the end when the third argument is true: 2.9.0 (39) debug. The third argument should be optional and false when left out.
hints: A format string does the first part: "%s (%d)" % [version, code]. %s takes the text, %d the whole number.
Keep that in a variable, add " debug" to it with += when debug is true – mind the space – and return it.
explain: In a real game the third argument would be OS.is_debug_build(), so the label tells a debug build from a release one without anybody having to remember which they installed.

title: Bump the version
task:
Write bump(version, part), which returns the next version name. part is "patch", "minor" or "major":

  • bump("2.9.0", "patch") → "2.9.1"
  • bump("2.9.4", "minor") → "2.10.0" – the numbers after the one raised go back to zero
  • bump("2.9.4", "major") → "3.0.0"

parse_version from the tutorial is there for you.
solution:
extends Node

func parse_version(text: String) -> Array:
	var parts := []
	for piece in text.split("."):
		parts.append(int(piece))
	return parts

func bump(version: String, part: String) -> String:
	var p := parse_version(version)
	match part:
		"major":
			p = [p[0] + 1, 0, 0]
		"minor":
			p = [p[0], p[1] + 1, 0]
		_:
			p[2] += 1
	return "%d.%d.%d" % p

tests.label: bump("2.9.4", "minor") is "2.10.0" – nine becomes ten, the patch goes to zero

hints: p is an array of three ints: p[0] is major, p[1] minor, p[2] patch. A match on part keeps the three cases apart.
For "minor": p = [p[0], p[1] + 1, 0]. For "major": p = [p[0] + 1, 0, 0]. For a patch only p[2] += 1.
explain: Because the parts are numbers, 9 becomes 10 with no special case; a version is three counters, not a decimal. The last line works because % accepts an array holding one value for each %d.

title: Fix the bug: the tenth release
task: newest(versions) should return the latest version name in a list. It worked for months and then, at 2.10.0, began insisting that 2.9.0 was the newest. Find out why and fix it. parse_version is provided and correct.
hints: v and best are Strings, so v > best compares them as text, a character at a time. Which comes first as text: "2.1…" or "2.9…"?
Write the tutorial's is_newer(a, b) – parse both, compare number by number – and use if is_newer(v, best): in the loop.
explain: The bug hid for as long as every number had one digit, which is why it appeared on a release day rather than in testing. Bugs that wait for the tenth of something are worth a test of their own: the second check here, with 0.9.10, would have caught it.

title: Presets that agree
task:
A project's presets are given as an array of dictionaries, each with a "name", a "platform" and, for Android ones, a "code". Write two functions:

  • android_codes(presets) -> Array: the different version codes found in the presets whose platform is "Android", each once, smallest first. Other platforms are ignored.
  • next_code(presets) -> int: if every Android preset has the same code, that code plus one. If they disagree, or there is no Android preset at all, -1 – the release must not go ahead.
starter:
extends Node

const AGREE := [
	{"name": "Web", "platform": "Web"},
	{"name": "Android", "platform": "Android", "code": 39},
	{"name": "Android Phone", "platform": "Android", "code": 39},
]
const DRIFTED := [
	{"name": "Android", "platform": "Android", "code": 12},
	{"name": "Android Phone", "platform": "Android", "code": 10},
	{"name": "iOS", "platform": "iOS"},
]

func android_codes(presets: Array) -> Array:
	return []

func next_code(presets: Array) -> int:
	return -1

tests.label: android_codes(AGREE) is [39] – one code, listed once
android_codes(DRIFTED) is [10, 12], smallest first
next_code(DRIFTED) is -1: the presets disagree
no Android preset at all is also -1

hints: In android_codes, loop over the presets, skip the ones that are not Android, and append a code only if the list does not have it yet (codes.has(…)). codes.sort() puts them in order.
next_code can ask android_codes: exactly one distinct code means they agree, so if codes.size() != 1: return -1, otherwise codes[0] + 1.
explain: This is the check at the top of Little Hours' release script, and the numbers in DRIFTED are from its comments: the bundle preset had been raised to 12 by a script that only edited the first one it found, while the phone preset sat at 10. Counting distinct values is a neat way to ask "are these all the same?" about any list.

title: What is left to do
task:
A release is a list of steps, and some cannot happen before others. STEPS gives each step an "id" and the ids it "needs" first. done is an array of the ids ticked so far. Write:

  • next_steps(done) -> Array: the ids of steps that are not done yet and whose needs are all done, in the table's order. These are the things you could do right now.
  • broken(done) -> Array: the ids of steps that are ticked although something they need is not – a checklist that is lying. In the table's order.

A release is finished when next_steps is empty and so is broken.
starter:
extends Node

const STEPS := [
	{"id": "tests", "needs": []},
	{"id": "version", "needs": ["tests"]},
	{"id": "export", "needs": ["version"]},
	{"id": "sign", "needs": ["export"]},
	{"id": "notes", "needs": []},
	{"id": "upload", "needs": ["sign", "notes"]},
]

func next_steps(done: Array) -> Array:
	return []

func broken(done: Array) -> Array:
	return []

tests.label: with nothing done you can run the tests or write the notes
signed but no notes: the upload is not offered yet
an export ticked without the version raised is broken
broken() lists every lying tick, in the table's order

hints: Both functions ask the same question of a step – "is everything it needs in done?" – so write that once as a helper, needs_met(step, done), which loops over step["needs"] and returns false at the first one missing.

next_steps keeps a step when not done.has(step["id"]) and needs_met(step, done). broken keeps it when done.has(step["id"]) and not needs_met(step, done). Looping over STEPS gives the table's order for free.
explain: The order of a release lives in the data now, not in anybody's memory, and the same two functions would run a checklist of fifty steps. Little Hours' script holds its order the plainer way – as the order of the lines in a file – but it follows the same rule: nothing is uploaded that was not signed, nothing signed that was not tested.

title: Which mode?
task: A game looks at its user arguments to decide what to do. Finish mode_for(args): it returns "test" if the list contains "--test", otherwise "sizes" if it contains "--sizes", otherwise "play". If both flags are there, the tests win.

tests.label: with both flags, the tests win
a flag it does not know means play

hints: args.has("--test") is true when that word is somewhere in the list.
Check for "--test" first and return straight away; then "--sizes"; the last line is return "play".

title: A number after a flag
task:
Write number_after(args, flag, fallback), which finds flag in the list and returns the word after it as a float.

  • number_after(["--zoom", "2"], "--zoom", 1.0) → 2.0
  • if the flag is not in the list, or is the last word with nothing after it: fallback
  • a negative number makes no sense for a zoom: return 0.0 for it

tests.label: the flag may be anywhere in the list
no flag: the fallback
the flag as the last word: the fallback, and no error
a negative number becomes 0.0

hints: You need the position, not only the word, so loop with an index: for i in args.size():. The word after position i is args[i + 1] – but only if i + 1 < args.size().
float("1.5") turns text into a number, and maxf(0.0, x) gives whichever is larger, which lifts a negative to zero.
explain: This is Little Hours' _read_zoom_arg, made general. The check i + 1 < args.size() is the part people leave out: without it, a flag typed as the last word reads past the end of the list and the tool stops with an error where it should have shrugged.

title: Fix the bug: the checker that passes everything
task: off_grid(sprites, tile) should return the file names of sprites that do not fit the tile grid: any sprite whose width or height is not a whole multiple of tile, and any sprite with a width or height of zero or less. It has been letting bad sprites through. Find both faults and fix them.
solution:
extends Node

const SPRITES := [
	{"file": "bed.png", "w": 48, "h": 32},
	{"file": "lamp.png", "w": 16, "h": 40},
	{"file": "sign.png", "w": 20, "h": 20},
	{"file": "empty.png", "w": 0, "h": 16},
]

func off_grid(sprites: Array, tile: int) -> Array:
	var out := []
	for sprite in sprites:
		var w: int = sprite["w"]
		var h: int = sprite["h"]
		if w <= 0 or h <= 0 or w % tile != 0 or h % tile != 0:
			out.append(sprite["file"])
	return out

func _ready() -> void:
	print(off_grid(SPRITES, 16))

tests.label: a sprite wrong in height only is reported
a sprite wrong in width only is reported
a sprite with no height is reported
a sprite that fits is not

hints: Run it. The lamp is 16 by 40 and is not in the output. Its width is fine and its height is not – read the if aloud and listen for the word that should be "or".
The second fault: 0 % 16 is 0, so a sprite with no size at all counts as fitting perfectly. Add w <= 0 or h <= 0 to the condition.
explain: A checker with a bug is worse than no checker, because people stop looking. That is why the tests here feed it sprites that are wrong in one way at a time. When you write a checker, test it on data you have broken on purpose and make sure it complains.

title: Generate the catalogue
task:
A folder listing arrives as an array of file names. Turn it into the lines of a GDScript catalogue.

  • category_of(file): the part of the name before its first underscore – "Busk_Stand.png" → "Busk". A name with no underscore is "Misc".
  • catalogue_lines(files): an array of lines. First ## AUTO-GENERATED. Do not edit by hand. and const PIECES := [; then one line for each file ending in .png, in alphabetical order, made of a tab and {"k": "Busk_Stand.png", "c": "Busk"},; then a closing ]. Anything that is not a .png – notes, .import files – is left out.

tests.label: category_of("SI_Party_00.png") is "SI" – only up to the first underscore
FOLDER gives six lines: two of heading, three pictures, one closing bracket
the first picture line is Bazaar_Kiosk.png: sorted, with a tab in front
the same files in a different order give the same lines

hints: file.find("_") gives the position of the first underscore, or -1 if there is none; file.substr(0, n) is the first n characters.

In catalogue_lines, first collect the names where file.ends_with(".png") and sort() them. Then append a line for each. Single quotes let the line contain double quotes: '\t{"k": "%s", "c": "%s"},' % [file, category_of(file)].
explain: "Busk_Stand.png.import" contains .png but does not end with it, which is why the test is ends_with and not contains: every imported picture has such a neighbour, and a generator that listed them would double the catalogue. Sorting makes the output independent of the order the folder happened to be read in, so a run that changes nothing changes no lines.

title: Audit the art folder
task:
Two lists: used, the picture names the game's tables mention, and files, the pictures in the folder. Write audit(used, files), returning a dictionary with three arrays, each in alphabetical order with no name repeated:

  • "missing": names in used with no file – the game will show a blank
  • "unused": files nothing uses – dead weight in the download
  • "twice": names that appear more than once in used – probably a copy-and-paste slip

tests.label: unused is ["old_bed.png", "sofa.png"], in alphabetical order
bed.png is used twice and listed once
a missing name used three times appears once in each list
a tidy folder gives three empty lists

hints: Three empty arrays to start. Walk used once for missing and twice, then walk files once for unused. list.has(x) and list.count(x) answer the questions.
To avoid repeats, append only if not missing.has(file) (and the same for the other two). Call sort() on each list before putting them in the dictionary you return.
explain: This is a real tool: Little Hours' own pack tools refuse to remove a picture that the town's data or a script still names, and say which they kept. For a few hundred names has() inside a loop is fine. For tens of thousands you would put the names in a dictionary first, as the step-counting example showed, and the function's results would not change by a letter.

title: The best score, kept as JSON
task: A saved best score is a string, like {"best": 7}, kept between games (Chapter S). Write best_text(score: int, saved: String) -> String: it reads the best from saved (0 if saved is empty or is not a JSON dictionary with a "best"), and returns a new JSON string, {"best": N}, where N is the larger of that and score.

tests.label: nothing saved: the score is the best
a lower score leaves the best alone
a higher score replaces it
text that is not JSON is treated as nothing saved
so is JSON of the wrong shape

hints: JSON.parse_string returns null for text that is not JSON, and a dictionary only if the text was one. Check with typeof(data) == TYPE_DICTIONARY.
JSON numbers come back as floats: int(data["best"]), then maxi(best, score) and JSON.stringify({"best": …}).
explain: Everything that comes in from outside is untrusted, even your own file (Chapter S). Wiring this into the capstone is a short job: call best_text(caught, saved) on winning, keep the string in a variable, and show the best on screen.

title: A second level, from a table
task: Levels are data. LEVELS below lists them (level 1 is the first entry). Write level_for(n: int) -> Dictionary, returning the entry for level n, or the nearest valid one if n is below 1 or beyond the last. Then write is_last(n: int) -> bool, true when n is the last level or past it.

tests.label: level 1 is the first entry
level 2 is the second
below 1 gives the first
past the end gives the last
is_last is true for the last level and beyond

hints: The list starts at index 0 but the levels start at 1, so there is a minus one somewhere.
LEVELS[clampi(n, 1, LEVELS.size()) - 1] and n >= LEVELS.size().
explain: To use it in the capstone: let level_for(level) supply GOAL, TIME and FALL in place of the constants, move to level + 1 in restart() after a win, and go back to 1 after the last. Your game now has as many levels as the table has lines.

title: Fix the bug: a pause that does not pause
task: This game has a clock and a pause button, toggle(). The pause flag changes, and the clock runs on regardless. Fix _process so that while paused is true the clock does not move. play() is there to play frames for the checks; leave it and toggle() as they are.

tests.label: unpaused, a second passes
paused, a second passes and nothing moves
unpaused again, it carries on from where it stopped

hints: The first check passes already: the bug only shows when paused is true.
An early return at the top of _process, as in the capstone's phase != "playing" and Little Hours' night_held.
explain: One check at the top of the loop pauses everything below it. Pausing by switching off each thing separately is how pause buttons end up leaving one clock running. Engine-wide pausing exists too (get_tree().paused, with nodes choosing whether to obey it) and is worth a read in the manual.

title: Pause the capstone
task: This is the finished capstone. Add a pause: the jump action (Space) toggles a new variable paused while the game is being played. While paused, the clock, the player and the lantern stand still – and the game is still redrawn. Restarting must clear the pause. Take care not to let the same key press both restart and pause.
starter:
extends Node2D

const TIME := 20.0
const SPEED := 120.0
const FALL := 60.0
const GROUND := 160.0
const CATCH := 16.0
const GOAL := 5
const DROPS := [40.0, 200.0, 120.0, 280.0, 80.0]

var phase := "playing"      # "playing", "won" or "lost"
var time_left := TIME
var player_x := 160.0
var caught := 0
var drop := 0
var lantern := Vector2(DROPS[0], 0.0)

func _ready() -> void:
	position = Vector2.ZERO

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	if phase != "playing":
		if Input.is_action_just_pressed("ui_accept"):
			restart()
		queue_redraw()
		return
	time_left = maxf(0.0, time_left - delta)
	var dir := Input.get_axis("move_left", "move_right")

tests.label: one press of jump pauses
while paused, two more seconds do not drain the clock
or move the player
pressing again resumes, and the clock runs

hints: Pause needs one variable and one early return. Put the toggle where it can be reached only while phase == "playing" – after the game-over branch, which returns.
After the game-over block: if Input.is_action_just_pressed("jump"): paused = not paused, then if paused: redraw and return. Add paused = false to restart().
explain: The game-over branch returns before the pause code ever runs, so the press that restarts a game cannot also pause it. Order inside the loop is part of the design.

title: Challenge: a save you can trust
task: The game saves {"level": 2, "best": 14}. Anything can happen to a file between a save and a load. Write sanitise(text: String) -> Dictionary that always returns a dictionary with exactly two keys: "level" as an int from 1 to 3 (default 1) and "best" as an int that is never negative (default 0). Text that is not a JSON dictionary gives the defaults; a missing or non-numeric value is replaced by its default; out-of-range numbers are clamped; extra keys are dropped.

tests.label: a good save comes through
and its numbers are ints, not floats
garbage gives the defaults
so does JSON of the wrong shape
out-of-range numbers are clamped
text where a number should be is replaced, a missing key is defaulted
extra keys are dropped

hints: Parse; if it is not a dictionary, use {} so every get falls back. A small helper that turns "a number or anything else" into "an int or the default" will save you repeating yourself.
typeof(v) == TYPE_INT or typeof(v) == TYPE_FLOAT says it is a number; then int(v), clampi(…, 1, 3) and maxi(…, 0).
explain: That is Chapter S in twenty lines, and it is what stands between a hand-edited or truncated file and a crash on the first screen. Little Hours' own loader works this way: it never trusts a file it has not checked.
